name: TM4C1230C3PMI7R
title: Tiva C Series TM4C1230C3PM Arm Cortex-M4F microcontroller, 80 MHz, 32 KB flash, 12 KB SRAM, 2 KB EEPROM, 64-pin LQFP
summary: A 32-bit Arm Cortex-M4F microcontroller with a single-precision FPU, running at up to 80 MHz from 32 KB of flash, 12 KB of SRAM and 2 KB of EEPROM, with TivaWare driver library and boot loader in ROM. It carries eight UARTs, four SSI, six I2C and one CAN controller, two 12-bit 1 Msps ADCs over 12 inputs, two analog comparators, twelve 16/32-bit and 32/64-bit timers, a 32-channel µDMA and up to 49 GPIOs. It runs from a 3.3 V supply with an on-chip 1.2 V core LDO and comes in a 64-pin LQFP for -40 °C to 85 °C.

operation.text: The core reaches the peripherals over two on-chip buses: the Advanced Peripheral Bus (APB), the older one, and the Advanced High-Performance Bus (AHB), which gives faster back-to-back accesses.

A 32-bit Arm Cortex-M4F running at up to 80 MHz (100 DMIPS) with the Thumb-2 mixed 16/32-bit instruction set, single-cycle multiply, hardware divide, bit-banding, unaligned access, saturating arithmetic, 16-bit SIMD and DSP multiply-accumulate. It has a single-precision IEEE 754 FPU, a memory protection unit, separate instruction and data buses (Harvard), integrated sleep modes, and breakpoint and trace debug over serial wire. Flash runs single-cycle only up to a set clock frequency.

A 24-bit down-counter that wraps at zero and is cleared on a write; it serves as an RTOS tick (for example 100 Hz), an alarm on the system clock or a variable-rate timer, a counter for elapsed time, or a clock-source monitor.

The NVIC handles 66 interrupts and 7 system exceptions, each settable to one of eight priority levels and reprioritisable at run time. The core stacks and restores its state in hardware and fetches the vector in parallel; interrupt entry takes 12 cycles, or 6 when tail-chaining, both without FPU stacking. An external NMI signal is available.

The system control block reports implementation details and configures and reports system exceptions. The MPU follows the ARMv7 Protected Memory System Architecture: protection regions that may overlap, access permissions, and memory attributes exported to the system.

Single-precision add, subtract, multiply, divide, multiply-accumulate (fused MAC included) and square root, conversions between fixed and floating point, floating-point constants, denormals and every IEEE rounding mode. It holds 32 single-precision registers, also usable as 16 double-word registers, and has a decoupled three-stage pipeline.

12 KB of single-cycle SRAM at 0x2000.0000, reachable by the µDMA and with bit-band aliases for atomic bit access; 32 KB of single-cycle flash; 2 KB of EEPROM; and a ROM holding the TivaWare peripheral driver library, the TivaWare boot loader, AES tables and CRC routines.

The flash erases in 1-KB blocks, and an erased block reads all 1s. Pairs of blocks (2 KB) are protected together, as read-only (no erase or program) or execute-only (no erase or program, and readable only by instruction fetch, not by data reads or a debugger).

The ROM driver library initialises and controls the peripherals, polled or by interrupt, without special pragmas or assembly wrappers; the ROM boot loader can load an application and update firmware in the field. The AES package is based on LGPL source. The CRC routines validate a block of data, such as received messages, decompressed data or flash contents.

2 KB arranged as 512 32-bit words in 32 blocks of 16 words (64 bytes), with built-in wear levelling, access protection per block, a lock for the whole module or per block with a 32- to 96-bit unlock code, and a write-complete interrupt. Endurance per 2-page block runs from 500K writes (writing a fixed offset in alternate pages in a circle) to 15M operations (cycling through two pages).

One CAN 2.0 A/B controller at up to 1 Mbps, with 32 message objects each with its own identifier mask, a maskable interrupt, automatic retransmission that can be disabled for time-triggered CAN, loopback self-test and a FIFO mode. It connects to an external transceiver through CANnTX and CANnRX. On the bus, 1 Mbps reaches below 40 m; slower rates go further (125 Kbps at 500 m). A message carries 0 to 8 data bytes.

Eight 16C550-style UARTs (not register compatible): baud rates up to 5 Mbps at divide-by-16 and 10 Mbps at divide-by-8; 16x8 transmit and receive FIFOs with programmable depth and trigger levels of 1/8, 1/4, 1/2, 3/4 and 7/8; 5 to 8 data bits, parity even, odd, stick or none, 1 or 2 stop bits; line-break generation and detection; an IrDA SIR encoder/decoder up to 115.2 Kbps half duplex with 3/16 or low-power (1.41-2.23 µs) bits and a 1 to 256 divider for the low-power bit time; ISO 7816 smart card support; modem flow control on UART1; EIA-485 9-bit support; FIFO-level and end-of-transmission interrupts; separate µDMA channels for transmit and receive. Each UART has one combined interrupt from its maskable Rx, Tx, flow-control and error sources.

Six I2C modules, each master, slave or both at once, in master transmit, master receive, slave transmit and slave receive. Speeds: standard 100 Kbps, fast 400 Kbps, fast-mode plus 1 Mbps and high-speed 3.33 Mbps. Clock-low timeout interrupt, two slave addresses, glitch suppression, multimaster arbitration with clock synchronisation and 7-bit addressing. The master interrupts on the end or abort of a transfer; the slave interrupts on data sent or requested and on START and STOP.

Four SSI modules, master or slave, for Freescale SPI, MICROWIRE or TI synchronous serial frames of 4 to 16 bits. A slave can turn its output off so several slaves share one master. Transmit and receive FIFOs are each 16 bits wide and 8 deep. The bit rate comes from a programmable prescaler and divider on the module clock. Loopback test mode, FIFO and end-of-transmission interrupts, and µDMA with separate transmit and receive channels: receive bursts at 4 entries in the FIFO, transmit bursts when four or more entries are free.

A 32-channel Arm PrimeCell µDMA controller copies between memories, from memory to a peripheral or from a peripheral to memory, using basic, ping-pong and scatter-gather modes (up to 256 transfers from one request). Channels are dedicated to on-chip modules, with one each for the receive and transmit sides of a bidirectional module and one for software, with flexible assignment and two priority levels. Core accesses take priority over µDMA; RAM striping and bus segmentation reduce contention. Data sizes 8, 16 and 32 bits; transfer sizes in binary steps from 1 to 1024; address increment of byte, half-word, word or none; maskable requests; an interrupt per channel on completion.

System control holds the device identification (version, part number, memory sizes), power control (a fixed on-chip LDO, Sleep and Deep-Sleep with clock gating, software shutdown of single peripherals and memory, and 3.3 V brown-out detection that raises an interrupt or a reset), the clocks and reset reporting. Clock sources: the 16 MHz precision internal oscillator (PIOSC), ±3% over temperature and voltage and trimmable in 7 bits to ±1%, which software can power down; the main oscillator (MOSC), either an external single-ended clock into OSC0 or a crystal between OSC0 and OSC1; and the low-frequency internal oscillator (LFIOSC) used in power-saving modes.
Power-on reset, the RST pin, brown-out reset, software reset, watchdog reset and main-oscillator failure.

Six 16/32-bit blocks, each two 16-bit timers or one 32-bit timer or RTC, and six 32/64-bit wide blocks, each two 32-bit timers or one 64-bit timer or RTC. Modes: one-shot and periodic; general-purpose timer with an 8-bit (16/32-bit block) or 16-bit (wide block) prescaler; RTC from an external 32.768 kHz clock; input edge count and edge time capture; PWM with output inversion. Count up or down, twelve CCP pins per block type, daisy chaining, synchronised start, ADC trigger, stall on debug halt (not in RTC mode), measurement of the latency from interrupt to service routine, and a µDMA channel per timer that bursts on the timer interrupt.

A CCP pin is a timer input in capture mode (the timer value is stored on a programmed event) or compare mode (an interrupt when the count matches a stored value), or a PWM output in PWM mode, where the timer counts the system clock and the output follows the match against the match register.

Two watchdogs: WDT0 clocked from the system clock, WDT1 from the PIOSC. Each is a 32-bit down-counter with a load register, its own clock enable, an interrupt that can be masked or made non-maskable, a reset output with an enable, a lock register against runaway software and a stall on debug halt. It can interrupt on the first timeout and reset on the second.

Seven GPIO ports (A to G) on the APB give up to 49 GPIOs, the count depending on which peripherals take pins. Pins are 5 V tolerant as inputs (except PB0, PB1, PD4, PD5 and the analog inputs), Schmitt-triggered as digital inputs, and toggle every two clocks on the APB (every clock on the AHB). Interrupts on rising, falling or both edges or on high or low level, maskable; bit masking of reads and writes through the address lines; a pin can start an ADC sequence or a µDMA transfer. Pads have weak pull-up or pull-down, 2, 4 or 8 mA drive, up to four pads sinking 18 mA, slew-rate control at 8 mA, open drain and a digital-input enable.

Two 12-bit ADC modules, each up to one million samples per second, sharing 12 analog input channels and an internal temperature sensor, single-ended or differential. Each has four sample sequencers of one to eight entries with result FIFOs, triggered by software, timers, the analog comparators or GPIO, an optional sample phase shift from 22.5° to 337.5°, averaging in hardware over as many as 64 samples, a set of eight digital comparators, and a µDMA channel per sequencer using burst requests. The analog supply and ground are separate from the digital ones.

Two independent comparators, each driving a pin, an interrupt or an ADC trigger, with interrupt and ADC trigger logic set separately (an interrupt on a rising edge and an ADC trigger on a falling edge, for example). The test input is compared against its own external reference, a shared external reference or a shared internal programmable reference.

The SWJ-DP joins JTAG and serial-wire debug in one port with real-time memory access while the core runs. IEEE 1149.1-1990 TAP with a 4-bit instruction register; IEEE instructions BYPASS, IDCODE, SAMPLE/PRELOAD and EXTEST, and ARM instructions APACC, DPACC and ABORT. Debug units: flash patch and breakpoint (FPB), data watchpoint and trace (DWT), instrumentation trace macrocell (ITM), embedded trace macrocell (ETM) and trace port interface unit (TPIU).
64-pin RoHS-compliant LQFP, industrial ambient range -40 °C to 85 °C.

The core runs at up to 80 MHz (100 DMIPS) and supports unaligned data access and bit-banding. It is a three-stage Harvard pipeline running Thumb-2 code, with single-cycle and SIMD multiply and multiply-accumulate, saturating arithmetic, hardware divide and a single-precision FPU compliant with IEEE 754. Its interrupt controller is tightly coupled: it has an NMI and eight priority levels, stacks registers in hardware, can suspend load-multiple and store-multiple instructions, needs no assembler wrapper round a handler, chains one handler into the next without a full unstack, and works with the sleep modes including Deep-sleep.

Debug reaches the core and memory either by a classic four-wire JTAG port or by two-wire Serial Wire Debug, both handled by one CoreSight SWJ-DP block. For trace there are the Instrumentation Trace Macrocell, data watchpoints and a profiling unit; a Serial Wire Viewer streams software messages, data trace and profiling information out through a single pin (SWO). The Embedded Trace Macrocell gives full instruction trace.

The FPB offers up to eight hardware breakpoint comparators. The same comparators can remap up to eight words of program code: accesses to chosen addresses in the code region are redirected to a remap table in SRAM or another flash area, so code held in read-only flash can be patched.

The TPIU takes the trace data from the ITM over the ATB slave port, passes it through an asynchronous FIFO and a serializer, and drives it off-chip on the serial wire trace output (SWO) to a trace port analyzer. It is configured over its APB slave port.

Inside the core sit SysTick (a 24-bit down-counter usable as an RTOS tick or a plain counter), the NVIC, the System Control Block (implementation information, system control, and configuration and status of the system exceptions), the MPU (up to eight regions plus an optional background region) and the FPU (single-precision add, subtract, multiply, divide, multiply-accumulate and square root, fixed/float conversion and floating-point constants).

Thread mode runs application code and is the mode left after reset; Handler mode runs exception handlers and returns to Thread mode when done. Unprivileged code has limited MSR and MRS use, may not execute CPS, cannot reach the system timer, NVIC or SCB, and may be kept from some memory or peripherals; privileged code may use every instruction and resource. In Thread mode the CONTROL register sets the privilege level, and only privileged code may write it; Handler mode is always privileged. Unprivileged code passes control to privileged code with the SVC instruction.

Stacks are full-descending: the stack pointer holds the address of the last item pushed, and a push first decrements it, then writes. There are two stacks, main and process, each with its own pointer register. CONTROL picks which one Thread mode uses; Handler mode always runs on the main stack.
The core handles 32-bit words, 16-bit halfwords and 8-bit bytes, and also has 64-bit transfer instructions. Every instruction and data access is little-endian.

The map is fixed and spans 4 GB. The SRAM and peripheral regions each contain a bit-band area. Part of the private peripheral bus range holds the core peripheral registers. Reading or writing a reserved address gives a bus fault, and so does any write into the flash address range. Each module's registers sit at offsets from its base address.

Each region of the map, as set by the map and the MPU, has a memory type. Normal memory lets the core reorder accesses and read speculatively. Device memory keeps the order of accesses relative to other Device and Strongly Ordered accesses; Strongly Ordered memory keeps it relative to every access. A write to Device memory may be buffered, one to Strongly Ordered memory may not. The Execute Never (XN) attribute forbids instruction fetches; a fault is raised only when an instruction from an XN region is executed.

For ordinary loads and stores, accesses may complete in a different order from the program as long as the program's behaviour is unchanged; where the order matters, software places a barrier between them. Two accesses that both go to Device or Strongly Ordered memory are always seen in program order.

Programs may sit in the Code, SRAM or external RAM regions, but the Code region is the better place because the core fetches instructions and accesses data on separate buses at the same time. The MPU can override the default access behaviour. The core prefetches ahead of execution and also speculatively from branch targets.

Access order is not guaranteed by program order because the core may reorder accesses, has several bus interfaces, sees different wait states in different memories, and buffers or speculates some accesses. DMB makes outstanding memory transactions finish before later ones; DSB makes them finish before later instructions run; ISB makes later instructions see the effect of completed transactions. Uses: after changing MPU settings, a DSB (and an ISB when the MPU code was reached by a branch or call rather than by an exception); a DMB between changing a vector-table entry and enabling that exception; an ISB right after self-modifying code; a DSB after switching a memory map; a DSB after changing the priority of an exception that is pending or active. The SCB is Strongly Ordered, so its accesses need no DMB.

Each 32-bit word in a bit-band alias region stands for one bit of the matching bit-band region. The bit-band regions are the lowest 1 MB of the SRAM and of the peripheral area; each has a 32 MB alias. A word, halfword or byte access to an alias address becomes an access of the same size to the underlying memory, so it suits the access rules of the peripheral beneath. Writes through the alias are done as read-modify-write.

Only bit 0 of a word written into the alias matters: 1 sets the target bit, 0 clears it, and bits 31:1 are ignored, so writing 0x01 equals writing 0xFF and writing 0x00 equals writing 0x0E. Reading an alias word returns 0x0000.0000 when the target bit is clear and 0x0000.0001 when it is set. Direct byte, halfword and word accesses to the bit-band region behave as in the memory access table.
Memory is a linear array of bytes numbered upward from zero; bytes 0 to 3 hold the first word and 4 to 7 the second. Words are stored little-endian: the least significant byte at the lowest address.

Load-Exclusive and Store-Exclusive pairs (LDREX/STREX for words, LDREXH/STREXH for halfwords, LDREXB/STREXB for bytes) give non-blocking exclusive access for read-modify-write updates and semaphores. The store returns a status bit: 0 means the write was done, 1 means it was not and the whole sequence must be repeated. A load-exclusive must be paired with the matching store-exclusive. To take a semaphore: read it with a load-exclusive, and if free, write the claim value with a store-exclusive; a failed store means another process may have taken it in between. The core's exclusive monitor drops its tag on CLREX, on any store-exclusive whether or not it succeeds, and on any exception.

The NVIC and core prioritise and handle every exception in Handler mode. State is pushed to the stack on entry and popped at the end of the handler, with the vector fetched in parallel with the push, and back-to-back exceptions are tail-chained without saving and restoring state in between. Eight priority levels can be set on seven system handlers (through the SYSPRIn registers) and on 66 interrupts (enabled with ENn, prioritised with PRIn); levels can be split into preemption priority and subpriority. The highest programmable priority, 0, ranks fourth after Reset, NMI and Hard Fault, and 0 is the default of every programmable priority.

After software writes to clear an interrupt source, the NVIC may need several processor cycles to see the request drop. If the clear is the last thing a handler does, the handler can return while the NVIC still sees the request and be entered again for nothing. Clearing the source early in the handler, or following the clearing write with another read or write to flush the write buffer, avoids this.

An exception is inactive (neither active nor pending), pending (waiting for service; a peripheral or software request makes an interrupt pending), active (being serviced; when one handler interrupts another both are active), or active and pending (being serviced with another request from the same source waiting).

Reset, on power-up or warm reset, stops the core anywhere, even mid-instruction, and restarts it privileged in Thread mode from the reset vector. NMI comes from the NMI signal or from software through INTCTRL; it is always enabled, fixed at priority -2, cannot be masked, and only reset preempts it. Hard Fault, fixed at priority -1, follows an error during exception processing or a fault no other mechanism can take. Memory Management Fault covers MPU and fixed protection violations on instruction and data accesses, and is used to stop fetches from XN regions even with the MPU off. Bus Fault (can be enabled or disabled) covers memory errors on fetches and data accesses. Usage Fault covers undefined instructions, illegal unaligned accesses, invalid state on execution and errors on exception return; unaligned word or halfword accesses and division by zero can also raise it when so configured. SVCall comes from the SVC instruction; Debug Monitor from the debug monitor when not halting, only when enabled and of higher priority than the current activation; PendSV is a pendable request for system service, typically for context switching, set through INTCTRL; SysTick comes from the system timer reaching zero or from software through INTCTRL. Interrupts (IRQ) come from peripherals or software through the NVIC and are asynchronous to execution. For asynchronous exceptions other than reset, one more instruction may run before the handler is entered. Privileged software can disable the exceptions that have configurable priority (SYSHNDCTRL and DIS0).

Interrupts (IRQx) are served by interrupt service routines. Hard, memory management, usage and bus faults are served by fault handlers. NMI, PendSV, SVCall, SysTick and the faults are system exceptions served by system handlers.

The vector table holds the reset value of the stack pointer followed by the start address of each exception handler, at the offsets in the exception and interrupt tables. Bit 0 of every vector must be 1, marking the handler as Thumb code. After reset the table is at 0x0000.0000; privileged software can move it by writing the VTABLE register to any address from 0x0000.0400 to 0x3FFF.FC00 on a 1024-byte boundary. The table runs to exception number 154 (IRQ 138) at offset 0x0268.

A lower priority number is a higher priority. Every exception except Reset, Hard Fault and NMI has a configurable priority, 0 by default; configurable values run from 0 to 7, so the three fixed negative priorities always win. Of pending exceptions with equal priority, the lowest exception number goes first. A running handler is preempted only by a higher priority; an exception of the same priority becomes pending, whatever its number.

Each priority field can be split into an upper group priority and a lower subpriority. Only the group priority decides preemption: an interrupt of the same group priority as the one running does not preempt it. Among pending interrupts with the same group priority the subpriority sets the order, and with both equal the lowest IRQ number goes first.

A higher-priority exception preempts a running handler and the two become nested. On return, if nothing pending has enough priority and no late arrival is being served, the core pops the stack and resumes the interrupted code. Tail-chaining skips the pop when another pending exception qualifies and goes straight to its handler. A late-arriving higher-priority exception that comes while state is still being pushed takes over the entry: the push carries on unchanged and the new vector is fetched; this can happen until the first instruction of the original handler reaches the execute stage, and ordinary tail-chaining applies when the late handler returns.

Entry happens when a pending exception has sufficient priority, meaning more than any limit set by PRIMASK, FAULTMASK and BASEPRI, and either the core is running Thread code or the newcomer outranks the active handler. A lower-priority exception stays pending. Unless tail-chained or late-arriving, entry pushes an eight-word stack frame (R0 to R3, R12, LR, the return address in PC, xPSR) on the current stack; when floating-point state is in use the frame also holds S0 to S15 and FPSCR, with an aligner word above as needed. After the push the stack pointer points at the lowest word of the frame. The vector is read while the frame is being pushed; then the handler starts, LR is loaded with an EXC_RETURN value saying which stack holds the frame and which mode the core was in, and the exception changes from pending to active. On a late arrival the earlier exception stays pending.

Return happens when Handler mode loads an EXC_RETURN value into the PC by POP or LDM that includes the PC, by BX with any register, or by LDR with the PC as destination. Bits 31:5 of EXC_RETURN are all ones; the low five bits choose the return stack and mode.

Faults are raised by a bus error on an instruction fetch, a vector-table read or a data access; by an error the core detects itself, for example an undefined opcode or a BX attempting a state change; by executing from an XN region; and by an MPU fault from a privilege violation or an access to an unmanaged region.

Every fault except Hard Fault has a configurable priority (SYSPRI1) and its handler can be disabled (SYSHNDCTRL). Normally priority and the mask registers decide whether a fault handler runs or preempts. A configurable fault is escalated to Hard Fault when a fault handler triggers another fault of its own kind (it cannot preempt itself), when a fault handler causes a fault of the same or lower priority, when any exception handler causes a fault of the same or lower priority than itself, or when the handler for the fault is disabled. A bus fault during the stack push on entry to the bus fault handler is not escalated: the handler runs with a corrupt stack. Only Reset and NMI preempt Hard Fault, and Hard Fault preempts anything except Reset, NMI and another Hard Fault.

A hard fault inside the NMI or Hard Fault handler puts the core in lockup, where it executes nothing until a reset, an NMI or a debugger halt. Lockup entered from the NMI handler is not left by a further NMI.

In Sleep only the processor clock halts. In Deep-sleep the system clock halts as well, and the PLL and flash are powered off. The SLEEPDEEP bit in SYSCTRL chooses which one is entered. Debug activity and other events can wake the core spuriously, so software must be ready to send it back to sleep, for instance from an idle loop.

WFI enters sleep at once unless a wake-up condition is already true. WFE checks a one-bit event register that software cannot read: at 0 the core sleeps, at 1 it clears the bit and carries on (the bit is typically set by SEV). With SLEEPEXIT set in SYSCTRL, the core goes back to sleep as soon as the last exception handler returns to Thread mode, so it runs only when an exception arrives.

From WFI or sleep-on-exit, the core wakes when the NVIC sees an exception with enough priority to be taken. Setting PRIMASK and clearing FAULTMASK lets it wake on an enabled higher-priority interrupt without entering the handler until PRIMASK is cleared, so restore work can run first. From WFE it wakes on any exception that would be taken; with SEVONPEND set in SYSCTRL, any newly pending interrupt wakes it too, even a disabled or low-priority one.

SysTick is a 24-bit down-counter that wraps at zero and is cleared by any write. It runs from the system clock or from PIOSC divided by 4 and stops if that clock stops in a low-power mode; it keeps running in Deep-sleep when CLK_SRC in STCTRL is set and PIOSCPD in DSLPCLKCFG is clear. Three registers: STCTRL (clock, enable, interrupt enable, status), STRELOAD (wrap value) and STCURRENT (count). Enabled, it counts down to zero, reloads from STRELOAD on the next clock and continues; a zero STRELOAD stops it at the next wrap. Reaching zero sets COUNT, which clears when read; writing STCURRENT clears it and COUNT without raising the exception. Reload and current values are undefined after reset, so set STRELOAD, write STCURRENT, then configure STCTRL. Use aligned word accesses. The counter does not move while the core is halted by a debugger. Uses include an RTOS tick (for example 100 Hz), an alarm on the system clock, a variable-rate alarm, a time measurement, and with the COUNT bit a check on whether work finished in time.

The NVIC takes 66 interrupts, each with a priority level of 0 to 7 where 0 is the highest, detects level and pulse interrupts, allows priorities to be changed on the fly, splits priority into group and subpriority, tail-chains interrupts, and has an external NMI. State is stacked and unstacked in hardware with no instruction overhead.

A level interrupt stays asserted until the peripheral drops it, usually when the handler services the peripheral; if still asserted on return from the handler it pends again and the handler runs again. A pulse (edge) interrupt is sampled on the rising processor clock edge and must be held for at least one clock for the NVIC to latch it. Entering the handler removes the pending state.

Every interrupt is latched. An interrupt becomes pending when the NVIC sees its signal high while it is not active, sees a rising edge on it, or software sets its set-pending bit (PEND0 and the others) or writes SWTRIG. It stays pending until the handler is entered, which makes it active: on return a level interrupt still asserted pends again, otherwise goes inactive; a pulse interrupt pulsed again during the handler becomes pending and active and pends again on return, otherwise goes inactive. Writing its clear-pending bit makes a level interrupt inactive only if the signal has dropped; a pulse interrupt goes inactive if it was pending, or active if it was active and pending.
The SCB gives implementation information and system control: configuration, control and status of the system exceptions.

The MPU splits the map into regions, each with its own location, size, access permissions and memory attributes; regions may overlap and attributes are exported to the system. There are eight regions, 0 to 7, plus a background region. Where regions overlap, the highest-numbered one applies. The background region carries the default map attributes but is reachable only by privileged code. Instruction and data accesses use the same regions. An access the MPU forbids raises a memory management fault; an OS can reprogram the regions for each process.

Disable interrupts before changing a region that handlers may use. All MPU registers need aligned word accesses except MPUATTR, which also takes byte or aligned halfword accesses; unaligned accesses are not supported. When reprogramming, disable regions not in use so old settings do not linger, and disable a region before rewriting it if it was enabled. A region is updated through MPUNUMBER, MPUBASE and MPUATTR, written one by one or with a multiple-word store; the MPUBASEx and MPUATTRx aliases let one STM program up to four regions. When MPUBASE carries the region number with VALID (bit 4) set, two words do the job. MPUNUMBER is at 0xE000ED98 and MPUBASE at 0xE000ED9C. The MPU registers sit on the strongly ordered PPB, so no barrier is needed while programming; a barrier is needed before setup if buffered writes may be affected, and after setup if later accesses must see the new settings (DSB, plus ISB when the code was reached by branch or call), unless setup is entered by an exception or followed by an exception return.

A region of 256 bytes or more is divided into eight equal subregions; setting a bit of the SRD field in MPUATTR disables one, the least significant bit standing for the lowest subregion. A disabled subregion lets an overlapping region match instead, and if none does the access faults. Regions of 32, 64 and 128 bytes have no subregions and need SRD = 0x00, or behaviour is unpredictable. Example: two regions share a base; region one is 128 KB and region two 512 KB; SRD = 0x03 on region two disables its first two 64 KB subregions so region one's attributes apply to the first 128 KB.
The TEX, S, C, B, AP and XN fields of MPUATTR set access to a region; an access without the needed permission gives a permission fault. Cacheability and shareability have no effect on this Cortex-M4.
An access that breaks the MPU permissions raises a memory management fault, and MFAULTSTAT records the cause.

The FPU executes 32-bit single-precision (C float) instructions, with fused multiply-accumulate for better precision; hardware conversion, add, subtract, multiply with optional accumulate, divide and square root; denormals and every IEEE rounding mode in hardware; a bank of 32 single-precision registers also usable as 16 doublewords; and a decoupled three-stage pipeline. It complies with ANSI/IEEE Std 754-2008. The doubleword view serves loads, stores and moves.

The extension register file is 32 single-precision registers, seen as S0 to S31, as D0 to D15 (64-bit), or as a mix. S<2n> is the low half of D<n> and S<2n+1> the high half; for example S12 and S13 are the halves of D6.

Full-compliance mode processes every operation to IEEE 754 in hardware. Flush-to-zero (FZ bit in FPSC) treats subnormal inputs of arithmetic CDP operations as zero, with exceptions from zero operands raised as usual, and replaces tiny results with zero; VABS, VNEG and VMOV are not arithmetic CDP operations and are unaffected. IDC flags an input flush and UFC a result flush. Default NaN mode (DN bit) makes any arithmetic operation with a NaN input, or producing a NaN, return the default NaN; only VABS, VNEG and VMOV keep the fraction bits of an input NaN.

With DN and FZ off, FPv4 operation complies with IEEE 754 in hardware with no support code. Not every IEEE 754-2008 operation is provided; missing ones include remainder, rounding to an integer-valued float, binary to decimal and decimal to binary conversion, and direct comparison of single with double precision. Fused MAC is supported. Library functions complete the standard.

A single-precision value with the maximum exponent and a nonzero fraction is a NaN: a 0 in the top fraction bit marks a signalling NaN, a 1 a quiet NaN, and two NaNs differing in any bit are different. In full-compliance mode NaNs follow the Arm Architecture Reference Manual: arithmetic CDP instructions process them in hardware, data transfers move them without raising Invalid Operation, and VABS, VNEG and VMOV copy them, changing the sign where the instruction says, without Invalid Operation. In default NaN mode arithmetic CDP instructions with NaN operands return the default NaN, and a signalling NaN sets IOC (FPSCR[0]).

Comparisons set flags in FPSCR; the VMRS APSR_nzcv instruction (formerly FMSTAT) copies them to the APSR so conditional instructions can test the IEEE predicates. Underflow uses tininess before rounding and loss of accuracy as an inexact result. In flush-to-zero mode, results tiny before rounding become zero and set UFC (FPSCR[3]). Outside it, subnormal operands are processed: a result that is not tiny is returned without UFC, with IXC (FPSCR[4]) set if inexact; a tiny result is returned as a subnormal or zero, setting UFC if also inexact.

Each instruction sets the cumulative exception flags in FPSCR as FPv4 defines; user-mode traps are not supported, the exception enable bits read as zero and ignore writes. Six core outputs, FPIXC, FPUFC, FPOFC, FPDZC, FPIDC and FPIOC, each follow one cumulative flag. Lazy stacking cuts exception latency by reserving stack space for the FP state without saving it.

The FPU is off after reset and must be enabled, from privileged code, before any floating-point instruction. Enabling for privileged and user code means setting bits 20 to 23 of CPACR (address 0xE000ED88) to turn on coprocessors CP10 and CP11 with a read-modify-write, then a DSB to let the store finish and an ISB to restart the pipeline.

The JTAG port (TCK, TMS, TDI, TDO) is an IEEE 1149.1-1990 compatible test access port: a TAP controller, a four-bit instruction register chain and data register chains, used for board interconnect tests, manufacturing information, pin observation and control, scan test and debug. Data shifts in on TDI and out on TDO. The device's JTAG controller sits beside the Arm JTAG controller in the core and multiplexes their TDO outputs: Arm instructions select the Arm TDO, the others the device's. Instructions: BYPASS, IDCODE, SAMPLE/PRELOAD and EXTEST from the standard, and APACC, DPACC and ABORT from Arm. Integrated Arm Serial Wire Debug comes with the SWJ-DP, the FPB for breakpoints, the DWT for watchpoints, triggers and profiling, the ITM for printf-style debug, the ETM for instruction trace, and the TPIU toward a trace port analyzer.

The JTAG/SWD signals are alternate functions of PC0 to PC3, but come out of reset in their JTAG/SWD role. They are commit-protected: making them GPIOs needs the GPIO lock and commit procedure. Selecting the debug function takes the AFSEL bit in GPIOAFSEL and the encoding 1 in the PMCn field of GPIOPCTL. All are TTL level.

The TAP controller is a state machine driven by TCK and TMS; the sequence of TMS values sampled on rising TCK edges decides when the chains capture, shift from TDI toward TDO, and update their parallel registers, and whether the instruction chain or a data chain is in use. The loaded instruction picks the data chain. EXTEST works on data already in a chain without capturing, shifting or updating. Unimplemented instructions decode as BYPASS, so TDI always reaches TDO. Of all reset sources only power-on reset and RST touch the JTAG module: both reset the pin configuration, but the internal JTAG logic is reset only by POR.

TCK clocks the test logic on its own, apart from the system clocks, so chained TAP controllers stay in step; it normally runs free at about 50% duty and may be stopped high or low for long periods without losing TAP state or register contents. TMS and TDI are sampled on the rising edge of TCK, so the standard expects them to change on the falling edge; TDO likewise changes on the falling edge, and is put in an inactive drive state when not shifting out, to save power. The pull-ups on all four are on after reset: on TCK this prevents stray clocking when nothing drives it, on TDO it holds a steady level when the port is idle. The pulls on TCK may be turned off to save power when TCK is always driven, and on TDO when High-Z is acceptable in some TAP states. Changes to Port C pull-up settings must leave the pull-ups on PC1/TMS and PC2/TDI enabled, or JTAG communication can be lost.

Power-on reset puts the TAP controller in Test-Logic-Reset. Afterwards, holding TMS high for five TCK cycles returns it there and resets the JTAG module and all its chains to default; this should be done to initialise the controller. The state machine is the IEEE 1149.1 one: Test-Logic-Reset, Run-Test/Idle, and for both the data and instruction paths Select, Capture, Shift, Exit1, Pause, Exit2 and Update.

Each register is a serial shift chain with a parallel load register. In the Capture states the chain samples its information, in the Shift states it shifts out on TDO while new data shifts in on TDI, and in the Update states the new data moves to the parallel register.

After POR or RST the four pins are in their JTAG/SWD setup: digital enable set in GPIODEN, pull-ups set in GPIOPUR, pull-downs cleared in GPIOPDR, alternate function set in GPIOAFSEL (bits 3:0 of Port C). Clearing AFSEL[3:0] makes them four extra GPIOs. Code in flash that switches them to GPIO at once can lock the debugger out, because it may not connect and halt in time; a routine that restores JTAG on an external or software trigger avoids this, and a locked part can be recovered with the flash programmer's Unlock function. The GPIO commit registers guard PC0 to PC3 and the NMI pins: writes to their bits in GPIOAFSEL, GPIOPUR, GPIOPDR and GPIODEN take effect only after GPIOLOCK is unlocked and the matching GPIOCR bits are set.

The debug clock and the system clock may differ. In Capture-DR the result of the previous transaction comes back with a three-bit ACK, which software should check before starting another transaction; with a system clock eight or more times faster than TCK or SWCLK, each operation is sure to be done in time and the ACK can be ignored.

If debug access is lost because software made the JTAG/SWD pins GPIOs, keeping RST asserted while the debugger alternates the two switch sequences, five of each, mass-erases the flash. Steps: assert and hold RST; apply power; send the first two steps of a JTAG-to-SWD change, then the first two of an SWD-to-JTAG change, and repeat until each has gone five times; release RST; wait 400 ms; power-cycle. The flash is erased first, then the non-volatile registers return to factory defaults; the EEPROM is wiped as well and its wear-leveling counts go back to factory state.

A serial-wire debugger connects without knowing JTAG by sending a preamble that walks the TAP from Test-Logic-Reset round the loop Run-Test/Idle, Select-DR, Select-IR, back to Test-Logic-Reset, three times; this enables SWD and disables JTAG. It is the one place the Arm TAP departs from IEEE 1149.1, and the sequence is unlikely in normal JTAG use. JTAG to SWD: TMS/SWDIO held high for 50 or more clocks, the 16-bit command 0xE79E (b1110.0111.1001.1110) sent LSB first on TMS/SWDIO, then TMS/SWDIO high again for 50 or more clocks (a line reset if SWD was already active); check with an SWD READID. SWD to JTAG: 50 or more clocks high, 0xE73C (b1110.0111.0011.1100) LSB first, at least 50 cycles high (Test-Logic-Reset if JTAG was already active); check by loading IDCODE into the IR and shifting out the DR.

After POR or RST the pins are set up for JTAG and need nothing. If the application made them GPIOs, JTAG returns only after PC[3:0] are given back their alternate function in GPIOAFSEL and any other pad settings on those pins are restored to default.

The IR and the six DRs are not memory mapped and cannot be reached from the APB; they are accessed serially through the TAP. The IR is a four-bit chain between TDI and TDO with a parallel load register; bits shifted in and updated become the current instruction.

EXTEST has no chain of its own: it drives the GPIO pads from the output and output-enable data preloaded in the boundary scan register instead of from the core, for connectivity tests, while the chain can still sample and load. SAMPLE/PRELOAD puts the boundary scan chain between TDI and TDO: in Capture-DR it samples the input, output and output-enable of every GPIO pad, shifts them out in Shift-DR while new data shifts in, and in Update-DR stores the new data for later use by EXTEST. ABORT, DPACC and APACC connect their chains to the Arm Debug Access Port's Abort register (to clear error bits or abort a request), its debug and status registers, and internal components and buses. IDCODE is loaded by POR and on entering Test-Logic-Reset and gives manufacturer, part number and version of the core. BYPASS makes the shortest path, a one-bit chain, to leave the device out of a test.

There are six data registers. IDCODE is 32 bits: version in bits 31:28, part number in 27:12, manufacturer ID in 11:1 and a 1 in bit 0, which tells it apart from BYPASS (bit 0 is 0). It reads 0x4BA0.0477, which lets debuggers configure themselves for the Cortex-M4F. BYPASS is one bit. The boundary scan register holds three signals per GPIO pin, in the order input, output, output enable, starting from a GPIO next to the JTAG pins; it is sampled on the rising TCK edge in Capture-DR. APACC, DPACC and ABORT are 35-bit registers defined by Arm in the Debug Interface v5 specification.

System control covers reset, NMI, power, clocks and low-power modes, and gives device information. NMI is an alternate function of PD7 or PF0 (GPIOPCTL encoding 8) and is a GPIO after reset; its pins are commit-protected, so selecting NMI or going back to GPIO needs the lock and commit procedure, with the AFSEL bit set in GPIOAFSEL. OSC0, OSC1 and RST are fixed pins.

Read-only registers report the version, part number, memory sizes and peripherals. DID0 and DID1 hold the version, package and temperature range among other things; Peripheral Present registers from System Control offset 0x300 (such as PPWD) say how many of each module the device has; each peripheral's Peripheral Properties register at offset 0xFC0 (such as GPTMPP) describes its capabilities. The older DC0 to DC9 registers remain for backward compatibility but say nothing of peripherals that older devices lacked.

Six sources: power-on reset; the RST pin; brown-out (VDD below BOR0 or below BOR1, each tripping at the highest VDD level of its band); software (the software reset registers); a watchdog timer reset; and a main oscillator failure.

After a reset the RESC register records the cause. Its bits are sticky across resets, except that an internal POR clears all of them but the POR bit; writing 0 clears a bit. On any reset that resets the core, a GPIO chosen in BOOTCFG can send the core to the ROM boot loader instead of the flash application: if EN in BOOTCFG is clear the ROM boot loader runs and compares the chosen pin with the chosen polarity; on a match the ROM is mapped to 0x0000.0000 and the boot loader continues. Otherwise, if the word at 0x0000.0004 is 0xFFFF.FFFF the ROM boot loader runs too; if not, SP is loaded from 0x0000.0000 and PC from 0x0000.0004 and the application starts. A device that fails its initialization toggles TDO as a debug sign. Example: BOOTCFG committed as 0x0000.3C01 makes PB7 the boot pin; PB7 low runs the ROM boot loader unconditionally, PB7 high runs the flash application if the reset vector is not 0xFFFF.FFFF, else the boot loader.

The internal POR circuit watches VDD and resets all internal logic, JTAG included, when the supply ramp reaches VVDD_POK; JTAG can only be reset by POR. The device must be within its operating conditions when the POR pulse ends. The sequence: wait for the internal POR to go inactive, release the internal reset, then load the initial SP, the initial PC and the first instruction, and run. The internal POR acts only on first power-up; RST can hold the device in reset longer.

RST resets the core and every on-chip peripheral. Its trace should be as short as possible and any parts on it close to the device. With only the internal POR in use, RST is tied to VDD through an optional pull-up of 0 to 100 kΩ. The input is filtered, so a pulse must last a minimum width to count. Sequence: RST held low for at least TMIN and let go; internal reset ends; the core fetches SP, PC and its first instruction and starts. An RC network on RST improves noise immunity or delays reset at power-up; a switch circuit gives a manual reset. In the switch circuit, RPU and C1 set the power-on delay.

Brown-out detection trips when VDD falls below the BOR0 or the BOR1 level. By default it causes a reset; clearing the BOR0 or BOR1 bit in PBORCTL makes that event raise an interrupt instead. RESC shows whether a reset came from brown-out. Sequence: VDD drops below VBORnTH and an internal BOR condition is set, an internal reset is asserted, then released, and the core fetches SP, PC and the first instruction and runs. The effect equals an RST assertion, and reset is held until VDD is back at a proper level.

A single peripheral is reset by setting and then clearing its bit in its software reset register; these begin at System Control offset 0x500 (SRWD for the watchdogs, for instance). SYSRESREQ in APINT resets the whole device including the core; VECTRESET in APINT resets the core only. Either way an internal reset is asserted and released, and the core loads SP, PC and the first instruction and runs.

There are two watchdog timers so one can cover the failure of the other's clock: one runs from the system clock, the other from PIOSC, and because that one is in another clock domain its register accesses must be spaced in time. A watchdog can raise an interrupt or an NMI at its first time-out and a reset at its second. After the first time-out the 32-bit counter reloads from WDTLOAD and counts down again; if it reaches zero again before the first interrupt is cleared and reset is enabled, the device is reset, with the same release sequence as the other resets.

Four sources raise an NMI: the NMI pin, a failed check of the main oscillator, software setting NMISET in INTCTRL, and a watchdog time-out when INTTYPE in WDTCTL is set. Software must find out which one it was. The NMI signal is an alternate function of PD7 or PF0, enabled in the GPIO with the lock and commit procedure; it is active high, and driving the enabled pin above VIH starts the NMI.

A verification circuit flags the main oscillator running too fast or too slow, outside the band of usable crystals. It is enabled by CVAL in MOSCCTL. On a failure the system clock moves to PIOSC automatically; with MOSCIM clear, MOSCFAIL in RESC is set, an internal power-on reset follows and the reset sequence goes to the NMI handler (keeping that code out of the normal reset handler); with MOSCIM set, MOFRIS in RIS is set to signal an interrupt instead.

An integrated LDO powers most internal logic; an external LDO may not be used. The LDO output VDDC feeds the internal logic and the PLL. VDD (+3.3 V) supplies the I/O buffers, and VDDA (+3.3 V) with GNDA supplies all analog circuits, the clock circuits included. VDDA must be within its specified range or the device does not work properly.

PIOSC, the precision internal oscillator, needs no external parts and is the clock during and after POR: 16 MHz, ±1% with calibration and ±3% over temperature; it can clock the ADC and the UART and SSI baud clocks whether or not it is the system clock. To use the main oscillator, software enables it after reset and lets it settle before switching. The main oscillator (MOSC) takes an external single-ended clock on OSC0 or a crystal across OSC0 and OSC1; with the PLL the crystal must be one of the supported values from 5 MHz to 25 MHz, without it from 4 MHz to 25 MHz (the supported list is the XTAL field of RCC). The low-frequency internal oscillator (LFIOSC) is meant for Deep-Sleep; its frequency varies widely, and using it lets MOSC and PIOSC be powered down there. The system clock can also come from the PLL output or from PIOSC divided by four (4 MHz ± 1%). The PLL reference must be 5 MHz to 25 MHz.

RCC and RCC2 control the system clock: the sources in Sleep and Deep-Sleep, whether the clock comes from the PLL or another source, which oscillators and the PLL are on, the dividers and the crystal choice. RCC2 widens some RCC fields, and when in use its fields override the matching RCC ones. Write RCC before RCC2. When moving the system clock onto MOSC, set MOSCDIS before reselecting MOSC, or the clock setup can sporadically end up undefined. Do not change the clock setup during an EEPROM operation: wait for WORKING in EEDONE to clear.

Peripherals run on the system clock and are gated one by one. The ADC clock comes from PIOSC, from the system clock when the PLL is off, or from the PLL output divided down to 16 MHz (÷25) when the PLL is on; an ADC not clocked from PIOSC needs a system clock of 16 MHz or more. The PLL runs at 400 MHz and is divided by 2 before SYSDIV unless DIV400 is set. The UART and SSI each have a clock control register at offset 0xFC8 selecting the system clock (default) or PIOSC as baud clock. RCC fields: XTAL, MOSCDIS, IOSCDIS, USESYSDIV; RCC or RCC2 (with USERCC2): PWRDN, BYPASS, OSCSRC; RCC2 only: DIV400; BYPASS, OSCSRC and the divider can also be set by DSLPCLKCFG in deep sleep; the CS fields of UARTCC, SSICC and ADCCC pick the module clocks.

The SYSDIV field of RCC sets the divisor (encoding plus one) applied to the PLL output or to the oscillator, depending on BYPASS; with the PLL the 400 MHz VCO is first halved. SYSDIV2 in RCC2 is two bits wider, giving divisors up to /64 for a lower clock and lower Deep-Sleep power. With DIV400 set, bit 22 (SYSDIV2LSB) becomes the LSB of SYSDIV2 and the divisor applies to 400 MHz directly, giving extra frequencies such as 80 MHz (/5); with DIV400 clear SYSDIV2LSB is ignored. DIV400 and SYSDIV2LSB are valid only with BYPASS2 = 0.

The device starts with PIOSC running. It must stay on even when another clock is chosen, since internal functions use it; it can be turned off only in Deep-Sleep, by setting PIOSCPD in DSLPCLKCFG. It is trimmed to 16 MHz at the factory and can be retrimmed for other voltages or temperatures: for the default calibration clear UTEN and set UPDATE in PIOSCCAL; for a user value set UTEN, write UT (a larger UT gives a longer period), then set UPDATE. The change completes within a few clock periods without glitches.
The main oscillator accepts a set of crystals from 4 MHz to 25 MHz. Software writes the crystal's number into the XTAL field of RCC; with the PLL in use, hardware turns that into the PLL settings.

The PLL is off after POR and is enabled by software when wanted; software picks the output divisor and lets the PLL drive the system clock. It runs at 400 MHz, halved before the output divisor unless DIV400 in RCC2 is set. OSCSRC2 = 0x1 in RCC2 makes PIOSC the PLL reference. With MOSC as reference, the hardware translation of XTAL into PLL settings, within ±1% of the target VCO frequency, can be read in PLLFREQn; it is redone whenever XTAL changes. Modes: Normal, multiplying the reference and driving the output, and Power-Down, with most of the PLL off and no output, both set in RCC/RCC2.

After a configuration change the PLL output is unstable until it relocks, which takes TREADY; meanwhile it cannot be used. Relock follows a change of XTAL in RCC (rewriting the same value does not count) and a move from Power-Down to Normal. A down-counter on the system clock times TREADY: it starts at 0x200 when the PLL powers up and at 0xC0 when M or N in PLLFREQn change; hardware keeps the PLL off the system clock until it expires. LOCK in PLLSTAT shows lock. Software must have a stable source (such as MOSC) before switching RCC/RCC2 to the PLL. If the PLL is enabled and selected in one step, the device keeps running from the chosen oscillator until TREADY is met, then switches; polling PLLLRIS in RIS or the PLL lock interrupt tells software when.

Per-peripheral clock gating registers (RCGCWD and its kin for Run, the SCGC set for Sleep, the DCGC set for Deep-Sleep) gate each module's clock in Run, Sleep and Deep-Sleep; they start at System Control offsets 0x600, 0x700 and 0x800. After a module clock is enabled in RCGC, wait 3 system clocks before touching the module's registers. The older RCGCn, SCGCn and DCGCn registers at offsets 0x100 to 0x128 remain for legacy code: writing one also writes the matching new bits, but a write through a new register to a legacy peripheral (such as TIMER0) is not reflected in the legacy register. Modules missing from the legacy registers need the new ones. Code mixing both should change the new registers only by read-modify-write touching peripherals absent from the legacy set; new code should use the new registers.

operation.topic: Wake-up with the debug port enabled
operation.text: If the Debug Access Port is enabled (usually by a debugger or flash programmer on JTAG or SWD), the core may start running after waking from Sleep or Deep-Sleep before all peripheral clocks are back to their Run settings, and touching a peripheral without a valid clock raises a hard fault. A delay loop at the start of the wake-up interrupt routine avoids it; it can be left out of production code, where the DAP is normally off. The DAP is off after power-on reset and is enabled only through JTAG or SWD, so a power cycle also clears it.
The core runs code and every peripheral enabled in its RCGC register runs. The system clock may be any source, the PLL included.

Entered with WFI. The processor and memory subsystem are not clocked, while active peripherals keep their clock frequency; the system clock keeps its Run source and frequency. Peripherals enabled in SCGC run when auto clock gating is on (RCC), or those enabled in RCGC when it is off. Any properly set up interrupt returns the device to Run mode. Lower-power SRAM and flash options exist at the cost of longer sleep and wake times. Before WFI, software must check that WORKING in EEDONE is clear.

Entered by setting SLEEPDEEP in SYSCTRL, then WFI; an interrupt returns to Run mode. The core and memory subsystem are unclocked, and peripheral clocks may change. Peripherals enabled in DCGC run with auto clock gating on, or those in RCGC with it off. DSLPCLKCFG sets the clock source: the chosen internal oscillator is powered if needed and other clocks are stopped. A running PLL is powered down and SYSDIV is overridden by DSDIVORIDE, up to /16 (RCC) or /64 (RCC2); the USB PLL is not stopped by WFI. On exit, hardware restores the earlier clock source and frequency before restarting the stopped clocks. PIOSC used as PLL reference may keep clocking in Deep-Sleep. Before WFI, WORKING in EEDONE must be clear. A communication module whose clock control register (offset 0xFC8) selects PIOSC as baud clock also takes PIOSC as its module clock in Deep-Sleep, so its FIFOs keep working; outside Deep-Sleep the module clock is the system clock.

In Sleep and Deep-Sleep, besides clock gating, the LDO, flash and SRAM can be put into lower-power states; SYSPROP says which options a device supports. LDOSPCTL and LDODPCTL set the LDO voltage in Sleep and Deep-Sleep, LDOSPCAL and LDODPCAL hold the factory-suggested values, SLPPWRCFG and DSLPPWRCFG set flash and SRAM power modes, DSLPCLKCFG sets the Deep-Sleep clock, and SDPMST reports status. Before lowering the LDO, software must set the clock for the lower voltage (RCC/RCC2 for Sleep, DSLPCLKCFG for Deep-Sleep). A value too low or too high is refused and reported in SDPMST. While JTAG is connected the Sleep and Deep-Sleep LDO settings are not applied.

operation.topic: Flash and SRAM power in sleep
operation.text: In Sleep or Deep-Sleep the flash may stay active or go to low-power mode; the SRAM may stay active or go to standby or low-power mode. Active modes sleep and wake fastest but draw the most; low-power modes draw least but take longest. SRAMSM in SYSPROP can forbid SRAM power management, behaving like the older Stellaris parts. Further SRAM options are retention and retention at a lower SRAM voltage, the latter lowest in power and slowest to sleep and wake. SLPPWRCFG and DSLPPWRCFG set flash and SRAM independently. Savings available: clock gating by SCGC or DCGC; in Deep-Sleep only, a different clock source and PIOSC off if no active peripheral needs it; a lower LDO voltage; flash low-power mode; SRAM standby or low-power mode. SDPMST holds the result of each power management request and some live status for a debugger or the core; it raises no interrupt, cannot be cleared and is overwritten by the next request.

Set up with direct writes to RCC/RCC2 (USERCC2 set to use RCC2 fields). 1: set BYPASS and clear USESYS in RCC so the device runs from the raw source while the PLL is set up. 2: choose XTAL and OSCSRC and clear PWRDN; writing XTAL loads valid PLL settings for that crystal and clearing PWRDN turns the PLL and its output on. 3: choose SYSDIV and set USESYS. 4: wait for lock by polling PLLLRIS in RIS. 5: clear BYPASS to run from the PLL.

An AHB peripheral at base 0x400F.9000 that handles the Cortex-M4 FPU's system-level exceptions; writes to functions a device lacks are ignored and reads return zero. All its events are ORed into one interrupt request, so one handler can serve several by reading SYSEXCMIS. SYSEXCIM chooses which events reach the interrupt controller; SYSEXCRIS always shows the raw status; writing 1 to a bit of SYSEXCIC clears it in both.

On chip: 32 KB flash, 12 KB SRAM with bit-banding, 2 KB EEPROM and a ROM. Flash erases in independent 1 KB blocks and is protected in 2 KB blocks. The EEPROM is reached through registers, by random word access or by sequential access, and blocks can be locked by password in 16-word units. The µDMA can move data to and from SRAM but cannot read flash or ROM, which sit on a separate internal bus.

SRAM starts at 0x2000.0000. Bit-banding gives atomic access to single bits through aliases, with the alias base at 0x2200.0000, saving read-modify-write sequences. The SRAM is two 32-bit banks, one holding the even words and one the odd words: a write followed at once by a read of the same bank stalls one clock, while a write to one bank and a read of the other run in consecutive clocks.

ROM starts at 0x0100.0000 and holds the TivaWare boot loader with its vector table, the TivaWare peripheral driver library for the device's peripherals, the AES cryptography tables and CRC error-detection functions. The boot loader loads a first program into empty flash and serves application-initiated firmware updates; the ROM driver library calls save flash.

The boot loader downloads code into flash without a debug interface. At reset any GPIO of Ports A to H, as set in BOOTCFG, can choose between the ROM boot loader and the flash application, by the sequence in the reset section. It uses a simple packet protocol, runs at the PIOSC speed (it does not start the PLL), and works over UART0, SSI0, I2C0 or USB; UART0, SSI0 and I2C0 share one data format and protocol, and USB uses the standard Device Firmware Upgrade class. The flash-resident version also supports CAN. The ROM boot loader does not drive U0Tx until autobauding is finished, so a floating U0Tx can look like characters to the receiver; a pull-up, which reads as idle, or a pull-down (reads as break) gives it a defined level, and the pull-up is the better choice.

driverlib/rom.h helps call the ROM copies of the driver library functions; driverlib/rom_map.h routes each call to ROM when the function is there on a given device and to a flash copy otherwise. A two-level table at the start of ROM points to the API entry points (one pointer per peripheral to a table of one pointer per function); it begins at 0x0100.0010, just after the ROM vector table, and keeps its layout even if the functions move. Graphics and USB libraries exist but are not in ROM.

The ROM holds the four XySSL AES tables: forward S-box, reverse S-box, forward polynomial and reverse polynomial. The CRC functions check that data is unchanged, after transfer, after decompression or in flash, and catch changes more reliably than a simple checksum.

Flash reads in a single cycle at system clocks of 40 MHz and below. It erases in 1 KB blocks, every bit returning to 1; a 32-bit word is programmed by changing bits from 1 to 0; a write buffer programs 32 consecutive words in half the time of writing them one at a time. Pairs of 1 KB blocks form 2 KB blocks that can be protected as read-only (no erase or program) or execute-only (no erase or program, and readable only by instruction fetch, not by the core as data nor by a debugger).

Above 40 MHz the flash runs at half the system clock and a prefetch buffer is used automatically: it fetches two 32-bit words per clock so straight-line code runs without wait states. Branch speculation avoids reading the next pair on a recognised branch and short loops often stay in the buffer, so some branches take no wait state and others one.

Each 2 KB block has two policy bits, in FMPPEn and FMPREn. FMPPEn set lets the block be programmed or erased; clear, it cannot change. FMPREn set allows execution and reading by code or by a debugger; clear, it may only be executed. A data read of a read-protected block gives a bus fault. A program or erase of a program-protected block is refused and can raise an interrupt (AMASK in FCIM) to catch misbehaving code during development. Factory settings are 1 for all implemented banks: open access. Bits are changed by clearing them; the change acts at once but becomes permanent only when committed through FMC; an uncommitted 1-to-0 change is undone by a power-on reset.

Execute-only blocks keep code both unmodifiable and unreadable while debug stays available, for instance to ship protected code and let the end user add code in an open flash area. Compilers usually place literal constants between functions and load them with PC-relative LDR, a data read on the DCode bus that execute-only protection blocks, so the code fails. Remedies: a compiler that gathers literals into a separate section placed in read-enabled blocks (LDR offsets limit how far the pool may be, or a register can point to the pool base); a compiler that builds constants from instruction immediates; or either method by hand in assembly.

Read-only blocks cannot be reprogrammed or erased but stay readable by the core and the debug port. Clearing an FMPREn bit blocks every read of that block, data included, so needed data must not live there. Read-only suits code such as a boot loader that controls flash access when debug has been permanently disabled.

The DBG0 and DBG1 bits of BOOTCFG can turn the debug interface off for good, blocking JTAG and SWD access to the core and peripherals while standard IEEE instructions such as boundary scan still work. It cannot be undone, so some update path such as the boot loader should be in place first.

The flash controller signals the end of a program or erase, and an attempted program or erase of a 2 KB block protected by its FMPPEn bit. FCIM selects which events interrupt; FCRIS always shows raw status; writing 1 to a bit of FCMISC clears it in both.

Erase and program use FMA (address), FMD (data) and FMC (control). A device locked by deactivated debug needs the recovery sequence first. While flash is being written or erased, flash access stops, so instruction and literal fetches wait; code that must run meanwhile has to run from SRAM. Only erase turns bits from 0 to 1; a write that tries to turn a 0 into a 1 fails and changes nothing. A flash operation may start before Sleep or Deep-Sleep and finish during it; one queued behind an EEPROM access is started and finished after wake-up. The write key in WRKEY is 0xA442 or 0x71D5 depending on the KEY bit of BOOTCFG. Word program: write FMD, write FMA, write the key with WRITE in FMC, poll until WRITE clears. 1 KB erase: write the block address to FMA, write the key with ERASE, poll until ERASE clears or use the programming interrupt (PMASK in FCIM). Mass erase: write the key with MERASE, poll MERASE or use the interrupt.

A 32-word buffer (FWBn registers) programs two words at a time, so 32 words take as long as 16 single writes. FWB0 maps to the FMA address with bits 6:0 zero, FWB1 to FMA + 0x4 and so on; only registers written since the last buffered write are programmed, as shown by FWBVAL (bit n for FWBn). Steps: fill FWBn, write a 32-word-aligned address to FMA (bits 6:0 zero), write the key with WRBUF in FMC2, poll until WRBUF clears or wait for the PMIS interrupt.

FMPRE0, FMPPE0, USER_REG0 to USER_REG3 and BOOTCFG live in flash outside the main array and survive erase and mass erase. Bits only go from 1 to 0. Values are written to the register's own address (for BOOTCFG, to FMD), act at once (BOOTCFG only after commit and the next POR) and can be read back; to see the pending BOOTCFG value read FMD, since BOOTCFG returns the committed or default value. Until committed, a power-on reset brings back the last committed or default value; other resets do nothing. To commit: write the value, write the FMA value from the table, then write the key together with COMT in FMC; it takes as long as a normal flash write (TPROG64), finishing when COMT clears or by the PMASK interrupt. Committing a BOOTCFG bit already committed as 0 back to 1 sets INVDRIS in FCRIS. Once NW in BOOTCFG is committed as 0 BOOTCFG cannot change again. Committed values return to factory defaults only by the locked-device recovery sequence, which mass-erases the main flash first.

2 KB arranged as 512 32-bit words in 32 blocks of 16 words (64 bytes), with built-in wear leveling, per-block access protection, locking of the whole module or of single blocks by 32-bit to 96-bit unlock codes, and an interrupt on write completion. Endurance per two-page block: 500K writes when writing a fixed offset in every other page in a circular way, up to 15M operations when cycling through two pages. Access is random (read and write) or sequential. The system clock setup must not change while an EEPROM operation runs: wait for WORKING in EEDONE to clear.

Bytes and halfwords can be read at any alignment (the whole word is read and the rest ignored), but writes are whole words only, so a byte write is read-modify-write. EEBLOCK selects the block and EEOFFSET the word, checked for validity; EEOFFSET may be written at any time and steps on each access to EERDWRINC, wrapping inside the block without moving to the next block. A read of a block without permission returns 0xFFFF.FFFF; a write without permission gives an error in EEDONE.

After enabling or resetting the module, wait for WORKING in EEDONE to clear before touching any EEPROM register. A flash write or erase can interrupt an EEPROM write, which then resumes, lengthening it. EEPROM operations must finish, checked in EEDONE, before WFI enters Sleep or Deep-Sleep. Reads within a block run at full speed with wait states added automatically when the system clock is faster than the EEPROM. Writing EEOFFSET costs nothing; writing EEBLOCK is immediate but data in the new block is delayed 4 clocks while block information loads. Word writes take a variable time, between the EEPROM write time and its erase time; software can poll EEDONE or use the interrupt.

The module and each block can be locked by a password held in EEPASSn: one to three words, never a word of all ones. Block 0 is the master: its password guards the control registers and every other block. With a block-0 password the whole module is locked at reset; blocks 1 to 31 are unreachable and EEBLOCK cannot leave 0 until block 0 is unlocked. Every password-protected block is locked at reset. Unlocking means writing the password to EEUNLOCK one to three times, the EEPASS0 value always last (for 96 bits: EEPASS2, then EEPASS1, then EEPASS0). Writing 0xFFFF.FFFF to EEUNLOCK locks again, since it is never a valid password.

Per block, with no password set: free read and write (the default in that case), or read only. With a password: reads always, writes only while unlocked (the default in that case); reads and writes only while unlocked; or reads only while unlocked and no writes at all. Access can also be limited by processor mode to supervisor only (which also shuts out the µDMA and the debugger) or supervisor and user (default). If block 0 is supervisor-only the whole module is. Block 0's protection level is the floor for every block: with PROT = 0x1 on block 0, block 1 may be 0x1, 0x2 or 0x3 but not 0x0. With a master password, the stricter of block 0's and a block's own protection applies.

Any block but block 0 can be hidden, blocking every access until the next reset. Initialization code can read passwords, keys or hashes from a block and then hide it, isolating that data from the application, most usefully with debug disabled.
Once EEDONE reports a location written, its data is kept until the next write to it; power loss or reset after that point cannot corrupt it.

An interrupt can signal each change of EEDONE from working to done, whether by error or success, for data writes, password and protection writes, forced erase through EESUPP and mass erase through EEDBGME. It shares the flash interrupt vector; bit 2 of FCMISC shows that the EEPROM was the source.

The EEPROM is built on a flash bank with EEPROM-type cells and sector erase. Words are replicated within pages to reach 500K+ erase cycles, so each word has a latest version and a write puts a new version in a new place. Each sector holds two blocks; each block has room for the active copy and six redundant copies, and passwords, protection bits and control data are kept in the pages. When a page is full, a copy buffer takes the latest words, that page is erased and the words copied back, so data survives power loss even during an operation. If a programming error still happens, for example from a falling supply, EESUPP lets the operation be completed.

The copy buffer is used only when a word in a block has been written seven times and has no room left; if the buffer is itself full it must be erased first, adding time. EREQ in EESUPP shows that the buffer needs erasing, and writing START erases it at a convenient moment; EEDONE and EEINT show completion.

Mass erase through EEDBGME needs no EEPROM operation active and no EEPROM register change after the last operation, not even EEBLOCK or EEOFFSET. To ensure this, reset the module with R0 in SREEPROM, wait for WORKING in EEDONE to clear, then set ME in EEDBGME.

Data writes, password and protection writes and copy buffer erases are made of several steps; a normal write writes a control word then the data, and if the data step fails (for instance on a voltage drop) EEDONE reports it. A failed normal or password/protection write should be retried once the system is stable, which advances to the next location; multi-word passwords written outside manufacturing should be written in immediate succession, or partial unlock must be supported. A failure during a copy-buffer transfer or a copy buffer erase is tracked by control words, shown in EESUPP, and resumed by writing START. After a reset and before writing any data, read EESUPP: if PRETRY or ERETRY is set, set and clear R0 in SREEPROM, wait for WORKING to clear and check again, repeating the reset in rare cases; then rewrite the data that was being programmed.

None of these should happen in the middle of an EEPROM program or erase: SYSRESREQ, a peripheral software reset, a watchdog reset, a MOSC failure reset. WORKING in EEDONE shows whether one is running. Debuggers can cause such resets. A watchdog reset can instead be routed to an external reset through a GPIO.

Endurance counts per meta-block of two blocks: as writes the application can make, and as erases of the meta-block, so the write count depends on the pattern. One word can be written over 500K times, but that wears the whole meta-block, so writing one word 500K times and then a neighbour 500K times is not assured; writes should be spread in parallel. Sweeping all words more than 500K times works. Words can each exceed 500K writes when their write counts stay close, balanced within 7 writes.

Enable the module clock in RCGCEEPROM, then: wait 6 cycles plus call overhead; poll WORKING in EEDONE until clear (power-on initialization done); read PRETRY and ERETRY in EESUPP and stop with an error if either is set; reset the module with SREEPROM (System Control offset 0x558); wait 6 cycles plus overhead; poll WORKING until clear; read PRETRY and ERETRY again, error if set, otherwise the EEPROM is ready. Skipping these steps can cause wrong behaviour or permanent data loss on a later write. PRETRY or ERETRY set with a stable supply is fatal and most likely means the EEPROM has passed its write/erase lifetime; with an unstable supply, retrying once it settles may clear it. TivaWare implements this as EEPROMinit().

An Arm PrimeCell 32-channel DMA controller that copies between memories, from memory to a peripheral or from a peripheral to memory, in Basic, Ping-pong and Scatter-gather modes (up to 256 transfers from one request). Channels are set up and run independently; supported modules have dedicated channels, receive and transmit on separate channels, one channel is reserved for software, and any channel can take software requests. Two priority levels. µDMA bus access yields to the core, helped by RAM striping and peripheral bus segmentation. Items are 8, 16 or 32 bits wide; a transfer counts 1 to 1024 items in powers of two; source and destination addresses step by byte, halfword, word or not at all. Peripheral requests can be masked, and each channel has its own completion interrupt.

The controller always gives way to the core on the bus and uses idle bus cycles, so its transfers cost the rest of the system almost nothing; striping and segmentation often let core and µDMA transfer at the same time. It can reach SRAM but not flash or ROM. Channels are configured through control structures kept in system memory, which allows simple transfers, task lists of arbitrary transfers from one request, and ping-pong streaming. Each channel has an arbitration size: how many items move in a burst before priority is rearbitrated.

Each channel has up to five possible assignments, chosen by a 4-bit field per channel in the DMACHMAPn registers; encodings 0x5 to 0xF are reserved. For legacy code, encoding 0 equals a clear DMACHASGN bit and encoding 1 a set one; reading DMACHASGN returns 0 for a field of 0 and 1 for any other value. Channels marked Software may be assigned to peripherals later but are free for software now; channel 30 is dedicated to software.

Priority follows channel number, channel 0 highest, plus a per-channel priority bit giving default or high priority. A high-priority channel outranks every default one; among high-priority channels the number decides. DMAPRIOSET sets the bit and DMAPRIOCLR clears it.

Among requesting channels the highest priority is served; once started it moves a set number of items, 1 to 1024 per channel, before arbitration happens again. A large arbitration size on a low-priority channel delays high-priority ones, so low-priority channels should keep it small. It acts as a burst size. This arbitration is between channels, not for the bus: on the bus the core always wins, and the µDMA is held off whenever the core needs the same bus, even mid-burst.

Peripherals make single requests (ready for one item) or burst requests (ready for several), and some make both; when both are asserted on a channel set up for burst, burst wins. On a single request the µDMA moves one item and waits. On a burst request it moves the smaller of the arbitration size and the items left, and the burst runs to the end without interruption, even by a higher-priority channel; bursts finish faster than the same number of single transfers. The arbitration size should match what the peripheral can take per burst request, for a UART the amount its FIFO trigger level allows. Setting the channel's bit in DMAUSEBURSTSET ignores single requests.

Channel settings live in a control table in system memory: contiguous, anywhere, and aligned to 1024 bytes. Each channel has a primary control structure and an optional alternate one; primaries occupy the lower half and alternates the upper half. Simple modes use only the primary, so only the first half need be allocated; ping-pong and scatter-gather need the whole table. Unused parts of the table, including unused channels' structures and each structure's unused word, are free for the application. Each entry is 16 bytes, 16-byte aligned, and holds four words: where the source ends, where the destination ends, the control word, and one unused word. End pointers give the last address of the transfer, inclusive; for a non-incrementing source or destination such as a peripheral register they give that address. The control word sets source and destination data size and increment, items per arbitration, total items, the useburst flag and the transfer mode; the µDMA counts the size down to 0 and sets the mode to Stop when done, so the control word must be rewritten before each transfer, while the pointers can be left if unchanged. A channel is enabled with DMAENASET before a transfer, disabled with DMAENACLR, and disabled automatically at the end of a transfer.

Stop is a mode-field value, not a transfer: the channel does nothing and is disabled; the µDMA writes it at the end of every transfer. Basic transfers items while there are items left and a request is present, for peripherals that request whenever ready; it is wrong for a momentary request such as a software request, which then moves only ARBSIZE items. Auto runs the whole transfer once requested even if the request goes away, suited to software-triggered transfers and rarely to peripherals. Ping-Pong keeps data flowing: the primary and alternate structures are both set up, and when one finishes the µDMA continues with the other and raises an interrupt so the processor can refill the finished one, without end.
