Memory Scatter-Gather uses the primary structure to copy entries from a task list in memory into the alternate structure, then runs each one; every entry's mode is Scatter-Gather except the last, which is Auto, after which the µDMA stops and only then interrupts. The list can loop back by having the last entry rewrite the primary structure, and entries can trigger other channels by writing their software request or causing a peripheral request. Up to 256 transfers can follow one request. Peripheral Scatter-Gather works the same way, but each list entry waits for a new peripheral request, so data moves between scattered memory and a peripheral as it becomes ready; the end pointers in a task list point to the last location of each buffer.

Data size is 8, 16 or 32 bits and must be the same at source and destination. Source and destination addresses increment independently by byte, halfword, word or not at all; the increment need not match the data size but must be at least as large (8-bit data with word increment is allowed). Data must be aligned to its size in memory.

Each µDMA-capable peripheral has a single and/or burst request line asserted when it is ready. DMAREQMASKSET masks a channel's request and DMAREQMASKCLR unmasks it. A transfer starts when the request is unmasked, the channel set up and enabled, and the peripheral requests. A peripheral served by µDMA must have all its interrupts to the NVIC disabled. The controller raises an interrupt at completion.

One channel is reserved for software transfers and has its own completion interrupt. Software sets up and enables the transfer, then requests it through DMASWREQ, using Auto mode. Any free software channel can be started the same way. A peripheral channel can be used for software requests while its peripheral is not using µDMA; its completion interrupt then arrives on the peripheral's vector rather than the software one.

Depending on the peripheral, completion is reported at the end of the whole transfer or at a FIFO or buffer level. Completion interrupts come on the peripheral's own vector, so its handler must expect them; software-channel completions come on the dedicated µDMA software vector. While µDMA serves a peripheral, its normal transfer interrupts do not reach the NVIC (they still show in its own registers), so a large transfer gives one interrupt instead of many; unmasked error interrupts still get through. Each completion sets the channel's CHIS bit in DMACHIS, letting the handler tell a µDMA completion from a peripheral event; the completion request clears itself when the handler starts. With UART or SSI FIFO transfers, any interrupt from that module calls for checking its DMACHIS bit at the end of the handler and clearing it by writing 1. A bus or memory protection error disables the channel at fault and raises the µDMA error interrupt; ERRCLR in DMAERRCLR shows a pending error and is cleared by writing 1.

Once at start-up: enable the µDMA clock in RCGCDMA; set MASTEREN in DMACFG; write the control table base, aligned to 1024 bytes, to DMACTLBASE. The module clock must be on before any µDMA register is written.

Channel 30 is reserved for software; any channel whose peripheral is idle also serves. Example: 256 words between two buffers on channel 30. Channel attributes: bit 30 of DMAPRIOSET or DMAPRIOCLR for high or default priority; bit 30 of DMAALTCLR to use the primary structure; bit 30 of DMAUSEBURSTCLR to accept single and burst requests; bit 30 of DMAREQMASKCLR to accept requests. The structure sits at table offset 0x1E0: source end pointer = source buffer + 0x3FC, destination end pointer = destination buffer + 0x3FC, control word at 0x1E8 as in the table. Start by setting bit 30 of DMAENASET, then bit 30 of DMASWREQ. The processor is interrupted at the end if the interrupt is enabled; bit 30 of DMAENASET and the XFERMODE field both clear when the transfer is done.

A buffer of 64 bytes goes to a peripheral transmit FIFO with a trigger level of 4 on channel 7. Attributes are set as in the memory example using bit 7. The structure is at table offset 0x070: source end pointer = source buffer + 0x3F, destination end pointer = the peripheral's transmit FIFO register, control word at 0x078 as in the table. Since the FIFO triggers at 4, ARBSIZE is 4: a burst request moves 4 bytes and a single request one; setting bit 7 of DMAUSEBURSTSET keeps it to bursts only. Setting bit 7 of DMAENASET starts it; the µDMA moves data whenever the peripheral requests until all 64 bytes are sent, then disables the channel and sets XFERMODE to 0 (Stopped). Bit 7 of DMAENASET and XFERMODE show completion, and an enabled peripheral interrupt fires at the end.

8-bit data flows continuously from a peripheral receive FIFO (trigger level 8) on channel 8 into two 64-byte buffers, switching when one fills. Attributes as before using bit 8. Primary structure at table offset 0x080, alternate at 0x280; both source end pointers are the peripheral's receive register, the destination end pointers are buffer A + 0x3F and buffer B + 0x3F, and both control words start the same, as in the table. ARBSIZE is 8 to match the FIFO trigger; DMAUSEBURSTSET bit 8 restricts it to bursts. An interrupt handler is the best way to run ping-pong, though polling also works; it fires after each buffer. Enable with bit 8 of DMAENASET. On a request the µDMA fills buffer A with the primary structure, then switches to the alternate and fills B, marking the primary Stopped with an interrupt pending. In the handler: if XFERMODE of the primary control word (0x088) is 0, buffer A is complete, so process it and reprogram that control word; likewise for the alternate at 0x288 and buffer B.

Each 4-bit field of the DMACHMAPn registers selects the assignment of one channel, as listed in the channel assignment table. The µDMA registers are at offsets from base 0x400F.F000; the control table's location is chosen by the application.

Seven GPIO blocks, ports A to G, one per port, give up to 49 programmable pins, fewer as peripherals take them. Each pin is a GPIO or one of several peripheral functions. Pins tolerate 5 V as inputs, except PD4, PD5, PB0 and PB1, which are limited to 3.6 V. Ports A to G are reached over the APB. A pin can change every clock cycle on the AHB and every second cycle on the APB. Interrupts are maskable, on a rising, falling or either edge or on a high or low level. Address lines mask bits on reads and writes. A pin can trigger the ADC or the µDMA. Digital inputs have Schmitt triggers. Each pad has weak pull-up or pull-down, 2, 4 or 8 mA drive (up to four pads can sink 18 mA), slew-rate control at 8 mA, open drain and a digital input enable.

A digital alternate function is selected by setting the pin's GPIOAFSEL and GPIODEN bits and writing the function's number into the pin's PMCx field of GPIOPCTL. An analog signal is selected by clearing the pin's DEN bit in GPIODEN; analog pins also tolerate 5 V. The AINx inputs are protected against voltage above VDD up to the absolute maximum, but analog performance holds only for 0 V < VIN < VDD at the pad. Each pin is set up on its own. Out of reset most pins are tri-stated GPIOs (GPIOAFSEL, GPIODEN, GPIOPDR, GPIOPUR and GPIOPCTL all 0); the special-consideration pins may come up in another function or with commit protection, and return to that state on a power-on reset or RST.
The pins that can be JTAG/SWD signals and NMI (PC0 to PC3, PD7 and PF0) are commit-protected, and the commit procedure applies to them whichever alternate function they are given.

Every port is the same block; not every block has all eight pins. A pin's pad is driven by the selected peripheral or by GPIODATA and GPIODIR, through the mode control (GPIOAFSEL, GPIOADCCTL, GPIODMACTL), the commit control (GPIOLOCK, GPIOCR), the port control (GPIOPCTL), the interrupt control and the pad control (GPIODR2R, GPIODR4R, GPIODR8R, GPIOSLR, GPIOPUR, GPIOPDR, GPIOODR, GPIODEN, GPIOAMSEL). Pins that reach the ADC input multiplexer have an isolation circuit between pad and analog circuitry.

GPIODIR sets each pin as input (bit clear: GPIODATA captures the pin) or output (bit set: GPIODATA drives the pin). Code that turns the JTAG pins into GPIOs at once on start-up can lock a debugger out; a routine that restores JTAG on an external or software trigger avoids this, and the flash programmer's unlock function recovers a part that is locked out.

GPIODATA occupies 256 addresses: address bits 9:2 mask which data bits an access touches, so single pins are set or cleared in one write without read-modify-write. On a write, a data bit changes only when its address bit is set. On a read, a data bit whose address bit is clear reads 0. Writing 0xEB to GPIODATA + 0x098 writes bits 5, 2 and 1 only; reading GPIODATA + 0x0C4 returns bits 5, 4 and 0 with the rest 0.

Each port has one interrupt line to the interrupt controller, controlled by seven registers. GPIOIS selects edge or level, GPIOIBE single or both edges, GPIOIEV the polarity; GPIOIM masks. GPIORIS shows every pin meeting its condition, GPIOMIS only those passed on. A level interrupt must be held until serviced and its RIS bit clears when the level goes away; an edge interrupt's RIS bit is cleared by writing 1 to GPIOICR. Interrupts should be masked while GPIOIS, GPIOIBE or GPIOIEV are written, as a write can raise a spurious interrupt.

operation.topic: GPIO as ADC and µDMA trigger
operation.text: With a pin's bit set in GPIOADCCTL and unmasked in GPIOIM, an interrupt on that port sends a trigger to the ADC, which starts a conversion when ADCEMUX selects the external trigger. With Port B's GPIOADCCTL clear, PB4 still works as the external ADC trigger, as on earlier devices. GPIODMACTL likewise makes an unmasked pin's port interrupt a µDMA trigger.

Software control (GPIO mode, through GPIODATA) is the default for most pins; setting a GPIOAFSEL bit hands the pin to its alternate function, chosen among several by GPIOPCTL. A pin used as an ADC input needs its GPIOAMSEL bit set to turn off the analog isolation circuit.

Writes to the protected bits of GPIOAFSEL, GPIOPUR, GPIOPDR and GPIODEN for PC0 to PC3 (JTAG/SWD) and PD7 and PF0 (NMI) take effect only after GPIOLOCK is unlocked and the matching GPIOCR bits are set.

GPIODR2R, GPIODR4R, GPIODR8R, GPIOODR, GPIOPUR, GPIOPDR, GPIOSLR and GPIODEN set each pin's drive, open drain, pull resistors, slew rate and digital input enable. A pad cannot drive 5 V; with 5 V on an open-drain output through a pull-up, the output level depends on the pull-up.
GPIOPeriphID0 to GPIOPeriphID7 and GPIOPCellID0 to GPIOPCellID3 identify the block as a GPIO.

A port's registers are reachable through the APB aperture, compatible with earlier devices, or the AHB aperture, with the same register map and faster back-to-back access; the two are exclusive and GPIOHBCTL selects one per port.

Enable the port's clock in RCGCGPIO (SCGCGPIO and DCGCGPIO for Sleep and Deep-Sleep). Set direction in GPIODIR (1 output, 0 input). Choose GPIO or alternate function in GPIOAFSEL and, for an alternate function, its PMCx field in GPIOPCTL; GPIOADCCTL and GPIODMACTL make a pin an ADC or µDMA trigger. Set drive in GPIODR2R, GPIODR4R and GPIODR8R; pull-up, pull-down or open drain in GPIOPUR, GPIOPDR and GPIOODR, and slew rate in GPIOSLR. Set GPIODEN for digital use or GPIOAMSEL for the analog function. Set interrupt type, event and mask in GPIOIS, GPIOIBE, GPIOIEV and GPIOIM. Optionally lock the NMI and JTAG/SWD pin configuration through GPIOLOCK. To change edge or sense settings without false interrupts: mask the port in GPIOIM, set GPIOIS and GPIOIBE, clear GPIORIS, unmask.

Every GPIO block carries the full register set; bits with no pad behind them ignore writes and read nothing meaningful. Port A sits at 0x4000.4000 on the APB and 0x4005.8000 on the AHB; Port B at 0x4000.5000 on the APB.

Six 16/32-bit timer blocks and six 32/64-bit wide timer blocks. Each 16/32-bit block has two 16-bit timers, A and B, that run apart as timers or event counters or join as one 32-bit timer or 32-bit RTC; each wide block has two 32-bit timers that join as one 64-bit timer. Timers can trigger µDMA transfers, and on a time-out in one-shot or periodic mode an ADC conversion; the ADC triggers of all timers are ORed into the ADC, so only one timer should trigger it. SysTick is a separate timer.

16/32-bit blocks: 16- or 32-bit one-shot and periodic timers, a 16-bit timer with 8-bit prescaler, a 32-bit RTC from an external 32.768 kHz clock, 16-bit input edge-count and edge-time capture with 8-bit prescaler, and 16-bit PWM with 8-bit prescaler and output inversion. Wide blocks: the same at 32 or 64 bits, with a 16-bit prescaler and a 64-bit RTC. Counting is up or down. Twelve CCP pins serve the 16/32-bit timers and twelve the wide timers. Timers daisy-chain so one starts several timing events, start together on one clock cycle through synchronization, trigger the ADC, can stall while the CPU is halted in debug (not in RTC mode), can show the time from interrupt to service-routine entry, and each has its own µDMA channel with a burst request on its interrupt.

Each timer has a free-running up/down counter with prescaler, match, prescale-match, interval-load, value and snapshot registers. The even CCP pin serves Timer A and also takes the 32 kHz RTC clock through the RTC predivider; the odd CCP pin serves Timer B. Timers are clocked by the system clock.

Used apart, Timer A and Timer B count 16 bits in a 16/32-bit block and 32 bits in a wide block; joined they count 32 or 64 bits. The prescaler is usable only with the timers apart. Counting down in one-shot or periodic mode the prescaler is a true prescaler holding the low bits of the count; counting up it extends the timer and holds the high bits. In edge-count, edge-time and PWM modes it always extends the timer.

GPTMCFG, GPTMTAMR and GPTMTBMR configure a block. Joined, A and B run in one mode; apart, each takes any individual mode. After reset the block is inactive with control registers cleared; both counters, GPTMTAILR, GPTMTBILR, GPTMTAV and GPTMTBV are all 1s, and the prescale, prescale snapshot and prescale value registers are all 0s. Joined modes use only Timer A's control and status bits. Writing 0x4 to GPTMCFG splits the block. The time-out is 0x0 counting down and the GPTMTnILR (with optional GPTMTnPR) value counting up, except in RTC mode.

TnMR in GPTMTnMR picks one-shot or periodic, TnCDIR the direction. Setting TnEN in GPTMCTL starts the count from 0x0 up or from the load value down; with TnWOT set the timer waits for a trigger. At the time-out a down-counter reloads from GPTMTnILR and GPTMTnPR and an up-counter reloads 0x0; a one-shot timer then stops and clears TnEN, a periodic one runs on. In periodic snapshot mode (TnMR 0x2 with TnSNAPS) the count at time-out goes to GPTMTnR and the prescaler to GPTMTnPS, while GPTMTnV and GPTMTnPV keep the free-running values, giving the time from interrupt to service; snapshot is not available in one-shot mode.

At time-out the timer can raise an interrupt, drive the CCP output and give triggers: TnTORIS in GPTMRIS sets and holds until cleared through GPTMICR, and TnTOMIS in GPTMMIS follows when unmasked in GPTMIMR. With TnMIE set, a match of the count with GPTMTnMATCHR and GPTMTnPMR raises the match interrupt, whose status bits update only while TnMIE is set. TnOTE in GPTMCTL enables the ADC trigger, asserted only by a time-out in one-shot or periodic mode. The µDMA trigger is enabled by setting up the timer's µDMA channel.

Counting down, a new GPTMTnILR or GPTMTnPR loads on the next clock with TnILD clear, or after the next time-out with TnILD set; counting up, the new time-out takes effect on the next cycle. A write to GPTMTnV loads on the next clock either way. New GPTMTnMATCHR or GPTMTnPMR values apply on the next clock with TnMRSU clear, or at the next time-out with it set. With TnSTALL set and RTCEN clear the timer freezes while the debugger halts the processor; RTCEN set overrides TnSTALL.

The joined timer counts up. The first time RTC mode is chosen after reset the counter loads 0x1; later load values go to GPTMTnILR, and the counter starts from the loaded value and rolls over at 0xFFFFFFFF. The even CCP (CCP0) input must carry 32.768 kHz, divided down to 1 Hz for the counter. Setting TAEN starts the count from 0x1; a match with GPTMTnMATCHR sets RTCRIS in GPTMRIS while the count runs on until reset or TAEN is cleared; at the end of the range it rolls over to 0x0. RTCMIS follows when unmasked; RTCCINT in GPTMICR clears the flags. GPTMTnR and GPTMTnV always read the same. GPTMRTCPD holds the predivider. A coherent RTC value is read as: Timer B (B1), Timer A (A1), the predivider, Timer A again (A2) until A1 = A2, then Timer B again (B2) until B1 = B2. The RTC can also trigger the µDMA.

The input must stay high two system clocks after a rising edge, or low two clocks after a falling edge, to be seen, so the highest input frequency for edge detection is a quarter of the system clock. The count runs up or down over 24 or 48 bits, the prescaler holding the upper bits; TnCMR clear selects edge count and TnEVENT in GPTMCTL picks rising, falling or both edges. Counting down, the difference between GPTMTnILR/GPTMTnPR and GPTMTnMATCHR/GPTMTnPMR is the number of edges counted; counting up, the timer counts from 0x0 to the match value, and the load value must exceed the match value. Each edge on the CCP pin steps the count; at the match CnMRIS sets (CnMMIS when unmasked) and a µDMA trigger can be raised. Counting down, the timer then reloads and stops, clearing TnEN, and ignores edges until re-enabled; counting up, it reloads 0x0 and runs on. GPTMTnR and GPTMTnPS hold the event count, GPTMTnV and GPTMTnPV the free-running values; counting up, GPTMTnR and GPTMTnV both hold the count. With load 0x000A, match 0x0006 and both edges, four edges are counted and later edges are ignored.

The same two-clock high or low minimum applies, limiting edge detection to a quarter of the system clock. Counting up or down over 24 or 48 bits with the prescaler holding the upper bits, it starts at GPTMTnILR/GPTMTnPR counting down and at 0x0 counting up. TnCMR set selects edge time; TnEVENT picks rising, falling or both edges. On each selected edge the count is captured in GPTMTnR and GPTMTnPS, CnERIS sets (CnEMIS when unmasked) and a µDMA trigger can be raised; GPTMTnV and GPTMTnPV keep the free-running values. The timer keeps counting after a capture until TnEN is cleared, reloading at time-out. The count wraps modulo 2^24 with the prescaler or 2^16 without; where an edge may take longer, a periodic timer at the same rate with a higher-priority interrupt catches the miss: if its handler finds an edge-time interrupt pending, the captured count is reduced by 1 before use.

The timer is a 24-bit or 48-bit down-counter whose start value, and so period, is GPTMTnILR and GPTMTnPR; frequency and period are synchronous, so the output is glitch-free. Set TnAMS to 0x1, TnCMR to 0x0 and TnMR to 0x2. TnEN starts the count (or TnWOT waits for a trigger); at 0x0 it reloads and runs until TnEN is cleared. The output asserts at the start value and deasserts when the count equals GPTMTnMATCHR and GPTMTnPMR; TnPWML inverts it. Interrupts on rising, falling or both edges are chosen by TnEVENT and enabled by TnPWMIE, setting CnERIS (status updates only with TnPWMIE set); with the output inverted the edge sense reverses. GPTMTnR equals GPTMTnV and GPTMTnPS equals GPTMTnPV. Example: a 1 ms period at 66% duty from a 50 MHz clock uses GPTMTnILR = 0xC350 and GPTMTnMATCHR = 0x411A (33% with TnPWML = 1).

Timers synchronized through GPTMSYNC need TnPLO and TnMRSU both set to keep the CCP outputs glitch-free. With those set: if GPTMTnMATCHR is above GPTMTnILR the CCP output is set; if they are equal the CCP output is not set (with PLO 0 it would go high at the load and the match is in effect ignored); if GPTMTnILR is above the match, the pulse is 1 clock wide at ILR - 1, 2 clocks at ILR - 2, and GPTMTnILR clocks at a match of 0.

With TnWOT set, timer N+1 starts counting only when timer N in the daisy chain reaches its time-out; GPTM1 follows GPTM0, GPTM2 follows GPTM1 and so on. A joined Timer A (32-bit, or 64-bit in a wide block) triggers Timer A of the next block; a split Timer A triggers Timer B of its own block, which triggers Timer A of the next. TAWOT must never be set in GPTM0. Works in one-shot, periodic and PWM modes.
GPTMSYNC in GPTM0 makes selected timers act as at a time-out at the same moment, without an interrupt; a joined timer needs only its Timer A bit. The timers involved need a common clock source.

Each timer has its own µDMA channel; it makes a burst request on every raw interrupt condition, and the arbitration size should be the amount to move per timer event. For example a 10 ms periodic time-out with a 256-item transfer and burst size 8 moves 8 items per time-out until all 256 are done.

Writing 0x0 or 0x1 to GPTMCFG joins the timers, and GPTMTAILR/GPTMTBILR, GPTMTAR/GPTMTBR, GPTMTAV/GPTMTBV and GPTMTAMATCHR/GPTMTBMATCHR (each [15:0]) form 32-bit registers: a 32-bit write to GPTMTAILR writes GPTMTBILR[15:0]:GPTMTAILR[15:0], and 32-bit reads of GPTMTAR and GPTMTAV return GPTMTBR[15:0]:GPTMTAR[15:0] and GPTMTBV[15:0]:GPTMTAV[15:0].

operation.topic: Reading and writing 64-bit and 48-bit wide-timer values
operation.text: Joined or prescaled values in wide blocks are wider than the bus and must be accessed atomically. To read: read Timer B (or the prescaler), then Timer A, then Timer B again; if the two Timer B reads differ, repeat once. This applies to 64-bit reads of GPTMTAV/GPTMTBV and GPTMTAR/GPTMTBR and 48-bit reads of GPTMTAR/GPTMTAPS, GPTMTBR/GPTMTBPS, GPTMTAV/GPTMTAPV and GPTMTBV/GPTMTBPV. To write: Timer B (or the prescaler) first, then Timer A; for 64-bit writes of GPTMTAV/GPTMTBV, GPTMTAMATCHR/GPTMTBMATCHR and GPTMTAILR/GPTMTBILR and 48-bit writes of GPTMTAV/GPTMTAPV, GPTMTBV/GPTMTBPV, GPTMTAMATCHR/GPTMTAPMR, GPTMTBMATCHR/GPTMTBPMR, GPTMTAILR/GPTMTAPR and GPTMTBILR/GPTMTBPR. Two writes in a row to the 64-bit registers, or Timer A written before Timer B, sets WUERIS in GPTMRIS, which can become an interrupt; the prescaler registers report no such error.

Enable the block's clock with its TIMERn bit in RCGCTIMER or RCGCWTIMER, and for CCP pins the GPIO port's clock in RCGCGPIO, with the PMCn fields of GPIOPCTL set for the CCP signals. One-shot or periodic: clear TnEN; write 0x0000.0000 to GPTMCFG; TnMR = 0x1 (one-shot) or 0x2 (periodic); optionally TnSNAPS, TnWOT, TnMTE and TnCDIR; load GPTMTnILR; unmask interrupts in GPTMIMR; set TnEN; poll GPTMRIS or take the interrupt and clear by writing 1 to GPTMICR. A one-shot timer stops after time-out and is restarted by repeating the sequence.

The timer needs 32.768 kHz on an even CCP input. Clear TAEN; clear leftover GPTMTnMR bits from an earlier mode; write 0x0000.0001 to GPTMCFG; write the match value to GPTMTnMATCHR; set or clear RTCEN and TnSTALL in GPTMCTL; set RTCIM in GPTMIMR for interrupts; set TAEN. On a match RTCRIS sets and the count continues until Timer A is disabled or reset; RTCCINT in GPTMICR clears it. A new GPTMTnILR value restarts the count there, running to 0xFFFF.FFFF and rolling over.

Clear TnEN; write 0x0000.0004 to GPTMCFG; TnCMR = 0x0 and TnMR = 0x3; choose edges in TnEVENT; set the load and match registers for the count direction as in edge-count mode; set CnMIM in GPTMIMR for interrupts; set TnEN; poll CnMRIS or take the interrupt, clearing with CnMCINT in GPTMICR. Counting down, the timer halts once the set number of edges has arrived; to restart, clear TnEN and repeat from the edge selection.

Clear TnEN; write 0x0000.0004 to GPTMCFG; TnCMR = 0x1, TnMR = 0x3 and the direction in TnCDIR; choose the edge in TnEVENT; write the prescaler to GPTMTnPR if used; load GPTMTnILR; set CnEIM for interrupts; set TnEN; poll CnERIS or take the interrupt, clearing with CnECINT; read the event time from GPTMTnR. The timer keeps running after an edge; a new GPTMTnILR value (TnILD clear) changes the interval from the next cycle.

Clear TnEN; write 0x0000.0004 to GPTMCFG; TnAMS = 0x1, TnCMR = 0x0, TnMR = 0x2; set inversion in TnPWML; write GPTMTnPR if a prescaler is used; for interrupts set the event in TnEVENT and TnPWMIE; load GPTMTnILR and GPTMTnMATCHR; set TnEN. The period can be changed at any time through GPTMTnILR, effective the next cycle.

Two watchdogs that give a non-maskable interrupt, a normal interrupt or a reset on time-out, to recover from software faults or an external device that stops responding. WDT0 runs on the system clock and WDT1 on PIOSC; WDT1, in its own clock domain, has synchronizers and a WRC bit in WDTCTL that shows when a write has completed. Each has a 32-bit down-counter with a load register, its own clock enable, maskable interrupt with an optional NMI, a lock register against runaway software, a reset enable and stalling while the CPU is halted in debug. It can interrupt on the first time-out and reset on the second.

Enabling the counter also enables the watchdog interrupt; the first time-out comes when the count reaches zero, after which the counter reloads from WDTLOAD and counts again. INTTYPE in WDTCTL makes the interrupt an NMI. If the count reaches zero a second time before the first interrupt is cleared and RESEN is set, the watchdog resets the system; clearing the interrupt first reloads the counter. A write to WDTLOAD while counting reloads the counter but does not clear an active interrupt, which only WDTICR clears. Re-enabling the interrupt preloads the counter from WDTLOAD. Out of reset the watchdog is disabled; software may start it first thing in the reset handler.

WDT1 registers need a gap between back-to-back writes and between a write and a following read; reads in a row are unrestricted. WRC in WDT1's WDTCTL clears on a write and sets when it completes; software polls for WRC = 1 before the next access. WDT0 has no such limit.

Enable the clock with the Rn bit of RCGCWD. Load WDTLOAD; for WDT1 wait for WRC; set RESEN if resets are wanted; for WDT1 wait for WRC; set INTEN, which enables the watchdog and its interrupt and locks the control register. Writing any value to WDTLOCK locks all registers; writing 0x1ACC.E551 unlocks them. The watchdog is serviced by reloading WDTLOAD. WDT0 is at 0x4000.0000 and WDT1 at 0x4000.1000.

Two identical 12-bit converters, ADC0 and ADC1, share 12 analog input channels and an internal temperature sensor. Each has four programmable sample sequencers, one to eight entries long with result FIFOs, each with its own input choice, trigger, interrupts and priority; results can go to eight digital comparators per module instead, which check each value against two limits. The two modules take independent or common triggers on the same or different inputs, and a phase shifter delays sampling by 22.5° to 337.5°. Single-ended and differential inputs; up to 1 million samples per second; triggers from software, timers, analog comparators and GPIO; hardware averaging of up to 64 samples; analog power and ground separate from digital; a µDMA channel per sequencer with burst requests.

ADC0 and ADC1 run independently: each can run its own sequences, sample any channel at any time and raise its own interrupts and triggers. Each module has sample sequencers SS0 to SS3 with input multiplexer, control and FIFO status registers, trigger selection (ADCEMUX, ADCPSSI), a hardware averager, the FIFO block, the digital comparators, and interrupt control; VDDA and GNDA feed it.

Each sample sequence is a programmed run of back-to-back samples, so the ADC reads several inputs without being reconfigured or serviced. Each step sets the input, single-ended or differential mode, an interrupt on completion and whether it is the last step; the µDMA can move the results. The sequencers differ only in length and FIFO depth. Results sit in the low 12 bits of 32-bit FIFO entries.

ADCSSMUXn selects each step's input; ADCSSCTLn holds each step's control bits: temperature sensor, interrupt enable, end of sequence and differential mode. A sequencer is configured, then enabled by its ASENn bit in ADCACTSS, and started by its SSn bit in ADCPSSI; GSYNC and SYNCWAIT in ADCPSSI start sequences on both modules together. An input may appear more than once in a sequence, any steps may interrupt, and END may be set on any step (on the fifth step of SS0 to end there). Results are popped from ADCSSFIFOn, a circular buffer read at one address; ADCSSFSTATn shows head and tail pointers and FULL and EMPTY. A write to a full FIFO is dropped and flagged as overflow; ADCOSTAT and ADCUSTAT record overflow and underflow.

The control logic outside the sequencers handles interrupts, DMA, sequence priority, triggers, the digital comparators, sample phase and clocking, mostly at the 16 MHz ADC clock. Hardware sets the internal divider for 16 MHz when the crystal is selected with the PLL.

Sequencer and comparator settings decide which events raise raw interrupts; the MASK bits of ADCIM decide which reach the interrupt controller. ADCRIS shows raw status and ADCISC the enabled active ones. Writing 1 to a sequencer's IN bit in ADCISC clears it; digital comparator interrupts are cleared through ADCDCISC.

Each sequencer requests its own µDMA channel. Only burst requests are made, asserted when a step's interrupt bit (IE in ADCSSCTLn) is set. The arbitration size must be a power of 2 and the matching IE bits set: with SS0's channel at arbitration size four, IE3 and IE7 are set and a request comes every four samples.
Simultaneous triggers are served in the order set by ADCSSPRI, 0 highest to 3 lowest; active sequencers sharing a priority give inconsistent results, so each must have its own value.

ADCEMUX sets each sequencer's trigger: the processor (default, through the SSx bits of ADCPSSI), the analog comparators, a GPIO pin chosen in GPIOADCCTL, a timer, or continuous sampling. A continuously sampling sequencer can starve lower-priority ones and is normally set to lowest priority; with a digital comparator it can interrupt when an input reaches a voltage.

At the same sample rate the two modules can sample together or at one of 15 phase offsets: ADCSPC delays sampling in 22.5° steps up to 337.5°. Both modules sampling one input with ADC1 at PHASE 0x8 (180°) and starts synchronized by GSYNC and SYNCWAIT, the combined results double that input's sample rate (1 Msps at 16 MHz in the example); the steps are then 0.5 µs apart at 1 Msps. With ADCSPC 0x0 on both, the modules sample two signals (say AIN0 and AIN1) at the same moments. Two modules sampling the same signal need a phase lag on one so they do not sample at the same instant.

The module runs on 16 MHz from the PLL divided down (PLL ÷ 25 by default when the PLL runs), from PIOSC, or from a 16 MHz source on MOSC with the PLL bypassed. To use PIOSC: power up the PLL, select PIOSC in the CS field of ADCCC, then disable the PLL. To use MOSC: power up the PLL, enable the ADC clock, then disable the PLL and switch the system clock to MOSC. With PIOSC as its clock the ADC keeps running in Deep-Sleep. The system clock must be at least the ADC clock. Both modules share one clock source, chosen in ADC0's ADCCC, and run at the same conversion rate.

BUSY in ADCACTSS reads 0 when no conversion is running or about to start; it must read clear before the ADC clock is turned off in RCGCADC. DITHER in ADCCTL reduces random noise and keeps the ADC within its specified performance; it is off after reset and should be on, together with hardware averaging, when taking several consecutive samples.

Up to 64 samples are accumulated and averaged into one FIFO entry, cutting throughput by the number averaged (by 16 for 16 samples). Averaging is off by default and set in ADCSAC; there is one averager, so all inputs, single-ended or differential, get the same averaging. With ADCSAC 0x2 (4x) and IE1 set, the interrupt comes after the second averaged value is stored.

A 12-bit successive-approximation converter whose switched capacitor array both samples and holds the input and acts as the 12-bit DAC. At the input: source Rs and Cs, the pin with ESD clamps to GND only and a 5 V ESD clamp, leakage IL, then RADC and CADC of the converter. The ADC uses both the 3.3 V analog and 1.2 V digital supplies; its clock can be stopped when not converting. The inputs reach the converter through balanced paths that limit distortion and crosstalk.

The references are internal: VREFP is tied to VDDA and VREFN to GNDA. Results run from 0x000 to 0xFFF; single-ended, 0x000 is VREFN and 0xFFF is VREFP. The pads take voltages outside this range, but results are accurate only within the ADC input limits of the electrical characteristics; the result saturates outside VREFN to VREFP.

Setting a step's Dn bit in ADCSSCTLn makes it differential, with the pair chosen in ADCSSMUXn: pair 0 is inputs 0 and 1, pair 1 inputs 2 and 3 and so on; no other pairings exist. The even channel is VIN+ and the odd channel VIN-. VIND = 0 gives 0x800; VIND > 0 gives 0x800 to 0xFFF; VIND < 0 gives 0 to 0x800. Both inputs must stay between VREFN and VREFP. The differential range is -VREFD to +VREFD, a peak-to-peak swing of 2 × (VREFP - VREFN); reaching it needs VINCM very close to VREFCM, and any common-mode difference clips the signal and narrows the range.

Meant to tell the system when the die is too hot or cold for reliable operation. It has no enable: it holds the bandgap reference, which other analog modules also use, so it is always on. It is sampled in a sequence by setting the step's TSn bit in ADCSSCTLn.

Eight per module watch conversions without the processor. Values are compared with the limits in ADCDCCMPn and an interrupt or trigger is raised for the low, mid or high band, in one of four modes. The SnDCOP bits of ADCSSOPn send a step's result to its digital comparator instead of the FIFO. Each comparator has two outputs, an interrupt and a trigger, each with its own state machine on the same conversions. CIE in ADCDCCTLn starts the interrupt function, which interrupts once its condition holds, provided DCONSSx is set in ADCIM. Only one DCONSSn bit may be set at a time; more than one masks INRDC in ADCRIS and stops all sequencer interrupts. Interrupts are best enabled on alternate samples or at the end of the sequence.

The CIM field of ADCDCCTLn picks the mode. Always: asserts on every conversion meeting the condition. Once: asserts when a conversion meets it and the one before did not. Hysteresis-Always: asserts while conversions meet the condition, and keeps asserting afterwards until the opposite band is entered. Hysteresis-Once: asserts once when a conversion meets the condition, the previous one did not and the hysteresis is clear. The hysteresis modes work only with the low or high band, as clearing needs the mid band crossed and the opposite band entered.

COMP0 and COMP1 in ADCDCCMPn split the range into the low band (below COMP0), mid band (above COMP0, up to COMP1) and high band (COMP1 and above). They may be equal, giving two regions, but COMP1 must not be below COMP0, which gives unpredictable results. The CIC field selects the band: 0x0 low, 0x1 mid (Always and Once only), 0x3 high.

The PLL must be on and set to a supported crystal frequency in RCC; others can make the ADC misbehave. Enable the ADC clock in RCGCADC and the GPIO ports' clocks in RCGCGPIO; set the AFSEL bits of the input pins; clear their GPIODEN bits; write 1 to their GPIOAMSEL bits to turn off the analog isolation; change ADCSSPRI if needed (by default SS0 is highest and SS3 lowest). Each sequencer: clear its ASENn bit while programming it; set its trigger in ADCEMUX; set each step's input in ADCSSMUXn and control nibble in ADCSSCTLn, with END set on the last (without END the behaviour is unpredictable); set its MASK bit in ADCIM for interrupts; set ASENn. ADC0 is at 0x4003.8000 and ADC1 at 0x4003.9000; after the module clock is enabled, 3 system clocks must pass before its registers are accessed.

Eight UARTs. Baud-rate generator up to 5 Mbps at regular speed (divide by 16) and 10 Mbps at high speed (divide by 8). Separate 16 x 8 transmit and receive FIFOs, with programmable length down to one byte (a double-buffered interface) and trigger levels of 1/8, 1/4, 1/2, 3/4 and 7/8. Start, stop and parity bits; line-break generation and detection; 5 to 8 data bits; parity even, odd, stick or none; 1 or 2 stop bits. IrDA SIR encoder/decoder, selectable against plain UART I/O, up to 115.2 kbps half-duplex, with normal 3/16 and low-power (1.41 to 2.23 µs) bit durations and a reference-clock divider of 1 to 256 for the low-power duration. ISO 7816 smart-card support, modem flow control on UART1, EIA-485 9-bit support, FIFO-level and end-of-transmission interrupts. µDMA on separate transmit and receive channels: receive makes a single request when the FIFO holds data and a burst request at the FIFO level; transmit a single request when the FIFO has room and a burst request at the level.

The baud clock comes from the system clock or PIOSC through UARTCC and UARTCTL. The transmitter, with its SIR encoder, drives UnTx from the 16 x 8 transmit FIFO; the receiver, with its SIR decoder, fills the 16 x 8 receive FIFO from UnRx; the baud-rate generator is set by UARTIBRD and UARTFBRD.

Each UART converts parallel to serial and back; it works like a 16C550 but its registers differ. TXE and RXE in UARTCTL enable transmit and receive, both on after reset. UARTEN in UARTCTL must be cleared before the control registers are programmed; disabling during a transfer lets the current character finish. The SIR block, set through UARTCTL, connects to an infrared transceiver for an IrDA SIR physical layer. The transmitter sends a start bit, data LSB first, the parity bit and stop bits; the receiver starts on a valid start pulse and checks overrun, parity, framing and line break, storing that status with each character in the receive FIFO. A frame is a start bit (0), 5 to 8 data bits, an optional parity bit and 1 or 2 stop bits.

The divisor is 22 bits: a 16-bit integer in UARTIBRD and a 6-bit fraction in UARTFBRD, enough for all standard rates. The UART clock is the system clock by default, or PIOSC through UARTCC, independent of the PLL settings. The internal reference runs at 16x the baud rate (Baud16) or 8x with HSE set (Baud8), divided down for the transmit clock and used for receive error detection; HSE has no effect in ISO 7816 mode. UARTIBRD, UARTFBRD and UARTLCRH form one 30-bit internal register updated only on a write to UARTLCRH, so a divisor change takes effect after UARTLCRH is written: UARTIBRD and/or UARTFBRD (in either order), then UARTLCRH.

Two 16-byte FIFOs; the receive FIFO carries four more status bits per character. Writing the transmit FIFO with the UART enabled starts a frame with the UARTLCRH settings, and sending continues until the FIFO is empty. BUSY in UARTFR sets as soon as the transmit FIFO is not empty and clears only when it is empty and the last character, stop bits included, has left the shift register; it can show busy with the UART disabled. With the line idle high, a low starts the receive counter; the start bit is valid if still low on the 8th Baud16 cycle (4th Baud8 cycle with HSE set). Data bits are then sampled one bit period apart, parity checked if enabled, and the stop bit must be high or a framing error is recorded; each received word goes into the FIFO with its error bits.

The SIR block converts between the UART stream and a half-duplex SIR interface on UnTx and UnRx, with no analog processing on chip; an infrared transceiver completes the link. It cannot send and receive at once; the SIR physical layer needs at least 10 ms between transmitting and receiving, which software must provide, since the receiver can be biased or saturated by the nearby transmitter LED. Normal mode sends a 0 as a high pulse 3/16 of a bit period and a 1 as a steady low. Low-power mode sets the pulse to three periods of IrLPBaud16 (1.63 µs at a nominal 1.8432 MHz). In both modes a start bit counts if the decoder output stays low for one IrLPBaud16 period after the low was seen, so a normal-mode UART receives low-power pulses as short as 1.41 µs. ILPDVSR in UARTILPR must set 1.42 MHz < FIrLPBaud16 < 2.12 MHz, giving low-power pulses of 1.41 to 2.11 µs; pulses shorter than one IrLPBaud16 period are rejected and pulses over 1.4 µs accepted.

With SMART (bit 3) of UARTCTL set, UnTx is the bit clock and UnRx the half-duplex data line to the card; a GPIO can drive the card's reset and the other card signals come from the system. The clock is at most system clock / 16. UARTLCRH must be set for 8-bit words (WLEN = 0x3) with even parity (PEN and EPS set); 2 stop bits are used automatically and STP2 is ignored. A parity error during transmission pulls UnRx low in the second stop bit; the UART then aborts, flushes and discards the transmit FIFO and raises a parity error interrupt. It does not retransmit by itself.

As a DTE, U1CTS is Clear To Send and U1RTS Request To Send; as a DCE, U1CTS is Request To Send and U1RTS Clear To Send. Hardware flow control connects U1RTS to the other device's clear-to-send input and its request-to-send output to U1CTS. The transmitter sends only while U1CTS is asserted; U1RTS shows the receive FIFO state and stays asserted until the programmed watermark is reached. CTSEN (bit 15) and RTSEN (bit 14) of UARTCTL set the mode; with RTSEN = 1 the RTS bit of UARTCTL cannot change U1RTS and its state should be ignored. Software flow control uses the U1CTS interrupt (bit 3 of UARTIM), its status in UARTRIS and UARTMIS, cleared through UARTICR.

9BITEN in UART9BITADDR turns it on, for multi-drop links where a master addresses one slave or a set of them. Slaves read the ninth bit, in place of parity, as the address qualifier and compare an address byte with UART9BITADDR, extended to a set by the mask in UART9BITAMASK (0xFF by default: one address). On a match the UART interrupts and stores the following data bytes (ninth bit clear) in the FIFO; without a match it drops the address byte and the data after it. The receiver runs without parity in this mode. Transmitted bytes are data with the ninth bit clear; to send an address, software sets stick parity with odd parity for that byte. The address/data bit is not kept in the transmit FIFO, so software manages it; the address byte can be sent as a single then a burst transfer to keep the parity timing right.

Two 16 x 8 FIFOs, both reached through UARTDR: a read returns 12 bits, 8 data bits and 4 error flags; a write puts 8 bits in the transmit FIFO. Out of reset the FIFOs are off and act as 1-byte holding registers; FEN in UARTLCRH turns them on. UARTFR has the empty and full flags (TXFE, TXFF, RXFE, RXFF) and UARTRSR shows overrun (OE); with the FIFOs off, the flags follow the holding registers. UARTIFLS sets each FIFO's interrupt level separately: 1/8, 1/4, 1/2, 3/4 or 7/8 (at 1/4 the receive interrupt comes after 4 bytes); both are at 1/2 after reset.

Sources: overrun, break, parity and framing errors, receive time-out, transmit (at the TXIFLSEL level, or with EOT in UARTCTL set when the last bit has left the serializer) and receive (at the RXIFLSEL level). All are ORed into one interrupt request; UARTMIS shows which are pending, UARTIM enables them, UARTRIS shows raw status; RTIM must be set to see receive time-out status in either register. Writing 1 to UARTICR clears them. Receive time-out asserts when data sits in the receive FIFO and nothing more arrives for 32 bit periods (64 with HSE set), and clears when the FIFO is emptied or through UARTICR. Receive interrupt: with FIFOs on, RXRIS sets at the trigger level and clears when reads take the FIFO below it or by RXIC; with FIFOs off, it sets when the single location fills and clears on one read or by RXIC. Transmit interrupt: with FIFOs on, TXRIS sets when the FIFO passes down through the level, so the FIFO must be refilled past the level for another; it clears when writes take the FIFO above the level or by TXIC. With FIFOs off it sets when the location is empty and clears on one write or by TXIC.
LBE in UARTCTL routes UnTx back into UnRx inside the UART for diagnostics; set LBE first, then enable the UART.

UARTDMACTL enables µDMA on the receive (RXDMAE) and transmit (TXDMAE) channels. Receive: a single request whenever the FIFO holds data, a burst request at or above the UARTIFLS level. Transmit: a single request whenever the FIFO has a free location, a burst request when it holds fewer characters than the level. With DMAERR set, a receive error turns off receive DMA requests until the error interrupt is cleared. With µDMA on, the UART still interrupts at the FIFO trigger points on its own vector, so the handler must also handle µDMA completion. EOT in UARTCTL makes the transmit interrupt come only when the FIFO is empty and the last stop bit has left the serializer, ignoring TXIFLSEL. When a UART interrupt occurs during µDMA transfers, the UART's bit in DMACHIS is checked at the end of the handler and cleared by writing 1.

Enable the UART in RCGCUART and the GPIO port's clock in RCGCGPIO; set the pins' AFSEL bits; set drive current and slew rate as the mode needs; set the PMCn fields of GPIOPCTL. Example, 20 MHz UART clock, 115200 baud, 8 data bits, one stop bit, no parity, FIFOs off, no interrupts: BRD = 20,000,000 / (16 × 115,200) = 10.8507, so UARTIBRD DIVINT = 10 (0xA) and UARTFBRD DIVFRAC = integer(0.8507 × 64 + 0.5) = 54. Then: clear UARTEN; write UARTIBRD; write UARTFBRD; write UARTLCRH (0x0000.0060 for this format); set the clock source in UARTCC; optionally set up the µDMA channel and UARTDMACTL; set UARTEN.

Four synchronous serial interfaces, each a master or slave talking Freescale SPI, MICROWIRE or TI synchronous serial protocols. Programmable prescaler and bit rate; a transmit FIFO and a receive FIFO, each 16 bits wide and 8 deep; frames of 4 to 16 bits; internal loopback; FIFO-based and end-of-transmission interrupts. µDMA on separate transmit and receive channels: receive makes a single request when the FIFO holds data and a burst request at 4 entries; transmit a single request when the FIFO has room and a burst request when four or more entries are free.

The SSI baud clock comes from the system clock or PIOSC (SSICC) through the prescaler (SSICPSR). The transmit/receive logic drives SSInTx, SSInClk and SSInFss and reads SSInRx, fed by the 8 x 16 transmit FIFO and filling the 8 x 16 receive FIFO through SSIDR.

The SSI converts between serial and parallel; the CPU reaches data, control and status. Transmit and receive each buffer up to eight 16-bit values, and the FIFOs can be µDMA source and destination, enabled in SSIDMACTL. A clock divider and prescaler make the serial clock; rates of 2 MHz and more are supported, the limit set by the peripheral devices. The input clock is divided by an even CPSDVSR of 2 to 254 (SSICPSR) and then by 1 + SCR, 1 to 256 (SCR in SSICR0).

Transmit and receive FIFOs are each 16 bits wide and 8 deep, reached through SSIDR. Data written to the transmit FIFO is shifted out on SSInTx, as master or slave. A slave sends each time the master starts a transfer; with its transmit FIFO empty it sends the eighth most recent value written, or 0 if fewer than 8 values have been written since its clock was enabled in RCGCSSI, so valid data must be kept in the FIFO; an empty FIFO can raise an interrupt or µDMA request. Data from SSInRx is registered and loaded into the receive FIFO until the CPU reads it.

Sources: transmit FIFO half full or less, receive FIFO half full or more, receive time-out, receive overrun, end of transmission, and receive and transmit DMA completion. All are ORed into one request; the four maskable interrupts are enabled by setting their bits in SSIIM, and SSIRIS and SSIMIS show status. The data-flow interrupts are separate from the status interrupts so data can be moved at the FIFO levels. The receive time-out is 32 SSInClk periods (whether or not the clock is running), started when the receive FIFO goes from empty to not empty and reset if it is emptied first; the handler clears it through RTIC in SSIICR right after reading the FIFO, early enough that it is cleared before the handler returns. The EOT interrupt, valid in master mode only, says all data has gone, so the clock can be stopped or sleep entered, and since receive finishes at the same moment, received data is ready without waiting for the time-out. In Freescale SPI mode an on-chip slave SSI with EOT 0, fed by µDMA to an on-chip master through external loopback, raises EOT for every byte even with the FIFO full.

Frames are 4 to 16 bits, MSB first, in one of three formats chosen by FRF in SSICR0: TI synchronous serial, Freescale SPI or MICROWIRE. In all three SSInClk is held inactive while idle and toggles only during a transfer; the idle clock gives the receive time-out. In SPI and MICROWIRE, SSInFss is active low for the whole frame. In TI format SSInFss pulses for one clock before each frame, and both ends drive data on the rising edge and latch on the falling edge. MICROWIRE is half-duplex: the master sends an 8-bit control message, receives nothing meanwhile, and the slave answers one clock after the last control bit with 4 to 16 bits, a frame of 13 to 25 bits.

Idle: SSInClk and SSInFss low, SSInTx tri-stated. When the bottom transmit FIFO entry holds data, SSInFss pulses high for one SSInClk period and the value moves to the shift register; from the next rising edge the MSB goes out on SSInTx while the slave puts its MSB on SSInRx. Both sides clock bits in on falling edges; once the LSB is latched, the next rising edge moves the word into the receive FIFO. Back-to-back frames repeat the SSInFss pulse before each frame.

A four-wire interface with SSInFss as slave select; SPO and SPH in SSICR0 set the clock's idle level and phase. SPO clear holds SSInClk low when idle, SPO set holds it high. SPH clear captures data on the first clock edge, SPH set on the second, which matters most for the first bit. In all four modes SSInFss idles high and SSInTx is tri-stated; a master drives the SSInClk pad and a slave leaves it undriven. A transfer starts when the SSI is enabled with data in the transmit FIFO: the master pulls SSInFss low and enables SSInTx. SPO=0, SPH=0: half a clock later master data is on SSInTx, another half period later SSInClk rises; data is captured on rising and changed on falling edges. SPO=0, SPH=1: after half a clock both data lines are driven and SSInClk starts with a rising edge; capture on falling, change on rising edges. SPO=1, SPH=0: as SPO=0, SPH=0 with the clock inverted, capture on falling and change on rising edges. SPO=1, SPH=1: SSInClk starts with a falling edge; capture on rising, change on falling edges. A single word ends with SSInFss returning high one SSInClk period after the last bit is captured. With SPH = 0, SSInFss must pulse high between back-to-back words, as the slave select freezes the slave's shift register; with SPH = 1 it stays low between words. The receive line is undefined outside the data bits.

Half-duplex message passing: each transfer begins with an 8-bit control word from the SSI, during which nothing is received; the slave decodes it during a one-clock wait and replies with 4 to 16 bits. Idle: SSInClk low, SSInFss high, SSInTx tri-stated. A control byte written into the transmit FIFO starts the transfer: SSInFss falls, the bottom FIFO entry moves to the shift register and its MSB goes out on SSInTx; SSInFss stays low for the frame and SSInRx stays tri-stated meanwhile. The slave latches control bits on rising edges, drives its reply on falling edges, and the SSI latches it on rising edges. A single frame ends with SSInFss high one clock after the last bit, moving the data to the receive FIFO; the slave may tri-state its line on the falling edge after the LSB or when SSInFss rises. In continuous transfers SSInFss stays low and the next control byte follows directly after the received LSB. An SSI slave samples the first receive bit on the rising edge after SSInFss falls; a master with a free-running clock must give SSInFss a setup of at least 2 × tSSIClk before that edge and a hold of at least one tSSIClk after the edge before it.

SSIDMACTL enables µDMA on the receive (RXDMAE) and transmit (TXDMAE) channels, set after the µDMA channel is configured. Receive: a single request whenever data is in the FIFO, a burst request at 4 or more items. Transmit: a single request whenever a location is free, a burst request when 4 or more are free. Transfer completion interrupts arrive on the SSI vector, so the SSI handler must handle them; when an SSI interrupt occurs during µDMA transfers, the SSI's bit in DMACHIS is checked at the end of the handler and cleared by writing 1.

Enable the SSI in RCGCSSI and the GPIO port's clock in RCGCGPIO; set the pins' AFSEL bits; set the PMCn fields of GPIOPCTL; enable the pins' digital function in GPIODEN and set drive strength, open drain and pull-ups or pull-downs. Pull-ups avoid stray toggles that can upset a slave; with SPO holding SSInClk high, the SSInClk pin needs its GPIOPUR pull-up. Then: clear SSE in SSICR1; write SSICR1 = 0x0000.0000 for master, 0x0000.0004 for slave with output enabled or 0x0000.000C for slave with output disabled; select the clock source in SSICC; write the prescale divisor to SSICPSR; write SCR, SPH and SPO, FRF and the data size DSS to SSICR0; optionally set up µDMA and TXDMAE or RXDMAE; set SSE. Example, master, Freescale SPI with SPO=1 and SPH=1, 1 Mbps, 8 data bits, 20 MHz system clock: CPSDVSR = 0x2 and SCR = 0x9; SSICR1 = 0x0000.0000, SSICPSR = 0x0000.0002, SSICR0 = 0x0000.09C7, then set SSE.

Two-wire bidirectional bus (SDA data, SCL clock) for devices such as serial memories, networking devices, LCDs and tone generators, and for test and diagnostics in development and manufacturing. Each module is master or slave, transmits and receives in either role and can be master and slave at once: master transmit, master receive, slave transmit and slave receive. Bus rates: 100 kbps Standard, 400 kbps Fast-mode, 1 Mbps Fast-mode plus and 3.33 Mbps High-speed. Clock-low time-out interrupt, dual slave address, glitch suppression. The master interrupts when a transmit or receive completes or aborts on an error; the slave when data is sent or requested or on a START or STOP. As master it arbitrates and synchronizes clocks with other masters, and uses 7-bit addresses.

Each module has a master core (I2CMSA, I2CMCS, I2CMDR, I2CMTPR and its interrupt registers) and a slave core (I2CSOAR, I2CSCSR, I2CSDR and its interrupt registers), joined to the I2CSCL and I2CSDA pins through an I/O select.

Each module has master and slave functions and its own address; the master that starts a transfer drives SCL. SDA must be set as open drain. SCL must not be set as open drain, because of the circuitry for high-speed operation, though it behaves as one. Both lines need pull-up resistors to a positive supply, sized from the I2C-bus specification.

The bus is idle when SDA and SCL are both high. Each transfer unit is nine bits: eight data bits, MSB first, and an acknowledge bit; the number of bytes between START and STOP is unlimited. A receiver that cannot take another byte holds SCL low to make the transmitter wait. START is SDA falling while SCL is high and STOP is SDA rising while SCL is high; the bus is busy from START to STOP. SDA must be stable while SCL is high and change only while it is low.

The STOP bit decides whether a cycle ends or continues into a repeated START. A single transmit: write the address to I2CMSA with R/S clear, then the control register with ACK = 0 or 1, STOP = 1, START = 1, RUN = 1; on completion or abort the interrupt goes active and data can be read from I2CMDR. As master receiver, ACK is normally set so a byte is acknowledged automatically, and cleared when no more data is wanted. As slave, STARTRIS and STOPRIS in I2CSRIS flag START and STOP, and I2CSMIS can pass them on as interrupts.

After START the master sends a 7-bit slave address and a direction bit (R/S in I2CMSA): 0 the master sends, 1 it requests data. The master always ends a transfer with STOP, but can address another slave with a repeated START without a STOP, mixing receive and transmit in one transfer.

The master generates the acknowledge clock; the transmitter releases SDA and the receiver pulls it low to acknowledge, keeping to the data-validity rule. A slave that does not acknowledge its address leaves SDA high so the master can STOP. A master receiver acknowledges each byte and signals the last by not acknowledging it; the slave then releases SDA for the STOP or repeated START. With I2CSACKCTL the slave acknowledges or refuses each byte itself, holding the clock low after the last data bit until the register is written.

Master transmit: when idle, write the slave address and R/S to I2CMSA; write data to I2CMDR; with BUSY in I2CMCS at 0, write 0x3 to I2CMCS; then, without a STOP, write another address to I2CMSA and 0x3 again for the repeated START. Master receive is the same, reading data from I2CMDR.

A slave can stretch a transfer by holding SCL low. A 12-bit counter tracks the low time: its upper 8 bits are CNTL in I2CMCLKOCNT (greater than 0x01) and its lower 4 bits are 0. It loads at START and decrements at every falling edge of the master's internal bus clock, which keeps running at the I2C speed even while SCL is held, and reloads whenever SCL is released. At zero the master forces an abort by issuing a STOP when SCL and SDA are released. Example: at 100 kHz, 0xDA becomes 0xDA0, 3488 clocks, a total low time of 34.88 ms. CLKRIS in I2CMRIS and CLKTO in I2CMCS set at the time-out; CLKTO clears on a STOP or master reset. I2CMBMON shows the raw SDA and SCL levels. Recovery is left to software, often by toggling the pins to force a STOP. If the bus recovers during a burst, the master tries to finish it; a slave that kept its state carries on, one that was reset or idled by the STOP may NAK the first byte. Writing the STOP bit in I2CMCR in the time-out handler limits the master to one more byte before a STOP; resetting the I2C peripheral before recovering the bus avoids stray data.

With dual addressing off the slave acknowledges the OAR address in I2CSOAR; with OAR2EN in I2CSOAR2 set it also acknowledges OAR2. The legacy address cannot be disabled. OAR2SEL in I2CSCSR is set when the alternate address was acknowledged.

A master starts only on an idle bus. When two masters start within the START hold time, they arbitrate on SDA while SCL is high: the first to send a 1 while the other sends a 0 turns off its output and waits for the bus to go idle. Arbitration can run over the address bits and, when both address the same device, into the data bits. In multimaster use, GFE in I2CMCR enables glitch suppression on SCL and SDA, with width set by GFPW in I2CMCR2 in buffered system clocks; all signals are then delayed inside, so with GFPW = 0x7, 31 clocks are added to the transfer time.

Standard (100 kbps), Fast (400 kbps), Fast plus (1 Mbps) and High-speed (3.33 Mbps); pick the mode the other bus devices use. The three slower modes are set by the I2CMTPR value that gives that SCL frequency.

Supported as master and slave; HS in I2CMCS selects it. Data moves at the high rate with a 66.6%/33.3% duty cycle, while communication and arbitration run at the chosen Standard, Fast or Fast plus speed; with HS set, current-mode pull-ups are on. The SCL period follows the same equation with SCL_LP = 2 and SCL_HP = 1, and the HS bit in I2CMTPR must be set for the TPR value to apply. A master first sends a master code byte, 0000.1XXX, at Standard or Fast speed to warn slaves; no slave acknowledges it. Software puts the master code in I2CMSA and writes 0x13 to I2CMCS; transfers then run at the high rate with the normal I2CMCS commands, without HS, until STOP. A high-speed slave needs no extra software. High-speed reaches 3.4 Mbps with the right system clock and enough pull strength on SCL and SDA.

Sources: master transaction completed, arbitration lost, transaction error and bus time-out; slave transaction received or requested; STOP and START detected on the bus. Master and slave have separate interrupt signals, combined into one request to the interrupt controller. Master: IM in I2CMIMR enables it; on an interrupt software checks ERROR (the last transfer was not acknowledged) and ARBLST in I2CMCS before continuing; IC in I2CMICR clears it; I2CMRIS shows raw status. Slave: DATAIM in I2CSIMR enables the data interrupt; RREQ and TREQ in I2CSCSR say whether to read or write I2CSDR, and FBR sets with RREQ on the first byte received; DATAIC in I2CSICR clears it. STARTIM and STOPIM enable the START and STOP interrupts, cleared by STARTIC and STOPIC; I2CSRIS shows raw status.
LPBK in I2CMCR ties the master's SDA and SCL to the slave's inside the device, for testing without the pins.

Single-byte transmit, 20 MHz system clock: enable the I2C clock in RCGCI2C and the GPIO port's in RCGCGPIO; set the pins' GPIOAFSEL bits; set the SDA pin to open drain; set the PMCn fields of GPIOPCTL; write 0x0000.0010 to I2CMCR; for 100 kbps write TPR = 9 (0x0000.0009) to I2CMTPR; write 0x0000.0076 to I2CMSA (slave address 0x3B, transmit); write the byte to I2CMDR; write 0x0000.0007 (STOP, START, RUN) to I2CMCS; poll BUSBSY until clear; check ERROR for the acknowledge. High-speed, 80 MHz system clock: the same set-up with TPR = 3 (0x0000.0003) for 3.33 Mbps; put the master code in I2CMSA and write 0x13 to I2CMCS; later transfers run at the high rate until STOP is set in I2CMCS; poll BUSBSY and check ERROR. I2C0 to I2C3 are at 0x4002.0000, 0x4002.1000, 0x4002.2000 and 0x4002.3000, I2C4 and I2C5 at 0x400C.0000 and 0x400C.1000. After the module clock is enabled, 3 system clocks must pass before its registers are accessed. TivaWare's hw_i2c.h addresses the slave registers at offsets 0x800 to 0x818 as 0x000 to 0x018 from a slave base 0x800 above the module base.

CAN is a multicast shared serial bus for linking control units, built to survive electrically noisy surroundings over a balanced differential line such as RS-485 or twisted pair; begun in cars, it is also used in industrial and medical control. Up to 1 Mbps on networks shorter than 40 m; slower rates reach further (125 kbps at 500 m). The device has one CAN unit: protocol version 2.0 parts A and B, up to 1 Mbps, 32 message objects each with its own identifier mask, a maskable interrupt, automatic retransmission that can be turned off for time-triggered CAN (TTCAN), loopback for self-test, a FIFO mode that stores several message objects, and direct connection to an external CAN transceiver through CANnTX and CANnRX.
Control and status registers (CANCTL, CANSTS, CANERR, CANBIT, CANINT, CANTST, CANBRPE), two message interfaces (IF1 and IF2) and the message RAM of 32 message objects, with CAN Tx and Rx to the pins.

Data, remote, error and overload frames with 11-bit (standard) or 29-bit (extended) identifiers, at up to 1 Mbps. The unit has a protocol controller with message handler, the message memory and the register interface. A data frame carries data; a remote frame carries none and asks for a given message object to be sent. The protocol controller moves serial data on and off the bus and hands it to the message handler, which stores it in the matching message object by the filters and identifiers, and raises interrupts on bus events. The 32 identical message objects hold configuration, status and data; they are not in the memory map and are reached only through the two interface register sets, which allow parallel access, usually one for transmit and one for receive.

Enable the CAN clock in RCGC0 and the GPIO port's clock in RCGC2; set the pins' AFSEL bits and the PMCn fields of GPIOPCTL. Initialization starts when INIT in CANCTL is set by software or reset, or on bus-off, when the transmit error counter passes 255. While INIT is set no messages move and CANnTX is held high; configuration, message objects and error counters are kept, and some configuration registers are writable only in this state. Set CANBIT and configure each message object, marking unused ones not valid by clearing MSGVAL in CANIFnARB2; a used object must be fully initialized. INIT and CCE both set give access to CANBIT and CANBRPE. Clearing INIT leaves initialization; the bit stream processor then waits for 11 consecutive recessive bits (bus idle) before taking part. Message objects can be set up on the fly, but should all have identifiers or be not valid before transfers start; to change one during operation clear MSGVAL, change it, then set MSGVAL again. CAN0 is at 0x4004.0000; after its clock is enabled, 3 system clocks must pass before its registers are accessed.

The interface register sets CANIF1x and CANIF2x are independent and identical and can queue transactions with the message RAM. After INIT is cleared the unit synchronizes to the bus. Each received message passes the message handler's filter and, if accepted, is stored whole (all arbitration bits, the DLC and all eight data bytes) in the object named by MNUM in CANIFnCRQ; arbitration bits masked as don't-care by the MSK bits of CANIFnMSKn may be overwritten. The CPU can read or write any message at any time through the interface registers; the handler keeps data consistent. Objects serve one-off transfers or stay set up permanently, with only the data updated. A transmission sets TXRQST in CANTXRQn and NEWDAT in CANNWDAn; when several messages share one object, the object must be fully configured before each request. Any number of objects may request at once; they go in priority order by message object number, 1 highest and 32 lowest. Messages may be updated or invalidated while pending; data updated before its transmission starts replaces the old. With RMTEN in CANIFnMCTL set, a matching received remote frame sets TXRQST and the object answers or interrupts; CANIFnMSKn, enabled by UMASK, sets which identifiers count as matching, and MXTD in CANIFnMSK2 is set for 29-bit requests.

When the transmit shift register is free and no interface transfer is in progress, the message handler loads the highest-priority valid object with a pending request and starts sending, clearing its NEWDAT. After a successful send with no new data written meanwhile, TXRQST clears; with TXIE set, INTPND in CANIFnMCTL sets. A message that loses arbitration or meets an error is resent when the bus is free, after any higher-priority messages requested meanwhile.

In CANIFnCMASK set WRNRD and choose with MASK, ARB and CONTROL whether to transfer the identifier mask, DIR and MXTD, the ID, DIR, XTD and MSGVAL, and the control bits; with CLRINTPND and NEWDAT whether to clear those bits; with DATAA and DATAB which data to transfer. MSK[15:0] in CANIFnMSK1 masks identifier bits [15:0] of a 29-bit identifier (unused for 11 bits); MSK[12:0] in CANIFnMSK2 masks bits [28:16], and MSK[12:2] masks bits [10:0] of an 11-bit identifier; MXTD and MDIR include XTD and DIR in filtering. A mask of 0x00 passes all messages, and masks apply only with UMASK set in CANIFnMCTL. For a 29-bit identifier, ID[15:0] in CANIFnARB1 holds bits [15:0] and ID[12:0] in CANIFnARB2 bits [28:16], with XTD set; for 11 bits, ID[12:2] in CANIFnARB2 holds bits [10:0] with XTD clear. Set DIR (transmit) and MSGVAL. In CANIFnMCTL optionally set UMASK, TXIE and RMTEN; set EOB for a single object; set DLC[3:0] to the data size, without setting NEWDAT, MSGLST, INTPND or TXRQST. Load CANIFnDA1, CANIFnDA2, CANIFnDB1 and CANIFnDB2 (byte 0 in DATA[7:0] of CANIFnDA1); write the object number to MNUM in CANIFnCRQ; set TXRQST. A matching remote frame with RMTEN set also starts transmission.

Data bytes can be updated at any time without clearing MSGVAL or TXRQST. All four bytes of a CANIFnDAn/CANIFnDBn register must be valid before it is transferred: either write all four, or first read the object into the register. To update data only, set WRNRD, DATAA and DATAB, write the data registers, then the object number to MNUM; set TXRQST to send soon. Setting NEWDAT and TXRQST together keeps a transmission already in progress from clearing TXRQST; NEWDAT clears when the new transmission starts.

Once an incoming message's arbitration and control fields are in, the handler scans valid message objects from object 1 with the acceptance filter (masks enabled by UMASK) and stops at the first match. For a data frame it stores the data, all arbitration bits and the DLC, so the data stays tied to its identifier even with masks, and sets NEWDAT, which the CPU clears on reading; a message arriving with NEWDAT already set sets MSGLST, meaning the earlier data was lost. With RXIE set, INTPND sets and CANINT points to the object. The object's TXRQST should be cleared so it does not send a remote frame.

Message object number sets receive and transmit priority, object 1 highest and 32 lowest; pending transmissions go lowest number first, whatever their identifiers, separate from the identifier priority the bus enforces.

As for a transmit object, with WRNRD set to write the message RAM: set CANIFnCMASK, the masks in CANIFnMSK1 and CANIFnMSK2 (enabled by UMASK), and the identifier and XTD in CANIFnARB1 and CANIFnARB2 with MSGVAL set and DIR clear (receive). In CANIFnMCTL optionally set UMASK and RXIE, clear RMTEN, set EOB for a single object and set DLC[3:0], without setting NEWDAT, MSGLST, INTPND or TXRQST. Write the object number to MNUM; reception starts with the next matching frame. A stored data frame puts the DLC and eight data bytes in CANIFnDA1 to CANIFnDB2 (byte 0 in DATA[7:0] of CANIFnDA1); with a DLC under 8 the remaining bytes take unspecified values. Masks let one object receive a group of frames; MXTD is set when the object expects only 29-bit identifiers.

The CPU can read a received message at any time. Usually it writes 0x007F to CANIFnCMSK and the object number to CANIFnCRQ, which copies the whole message into the interface registers and clears NEWDAT and INTPND in the message RAM. With masks in use, CANIFnARBn shows the full received ID. NEWDAT shows a new message since the last read; MSGLST shows more than one, and software clears it. Setting TXRQST on a receive object sends a remote frame with its identifier to ask another node for data; if the data frame arrives before the remote frame is sent, TXRQST resets itself.

Receive objects joined into a FIFO are configured like single receive objects with matching identifiers and masks, and EOB clear on every member except the final one, whose EOB is set. The lowest-numbered object is the first entry. Matching messages fill the FIFO from the lowest number; an object with NEWDAT set and EOB clear is locked until the CPU clears NEWDAT. Until earlier objects are released, further messages overwrite the last object. To read, write the object number to CANIFnCRQ with TXRQST and CLRINTPND set in CANIFnCMSK so NEWDAT and INTPND clear after the read (the register shows their state before clearing); objects are read in rising number order. A new message goes to the lowest object with NEWDAT clear, so the order in the FIFO is not guaranteed. A handler reads the interrupt pointer: 0x8000 is a status change, 0x0000 none, otherwise it reads objects from that number, reading data while NEWDAT = 1, until the object with EOB = 1.

CANINT points to the highest-priority pending interrupt, whatever the order of arrival: the status interrupt first, then message interrupts by lowest object number. A message interrupt clears when the object's INTPND is cleared or CANSTS is read; the status interrupt clears only by reading CANSTS (a write can clear RXOK, TXOK and LEC). INTID reads 0x0000 when nothing is pending; anything else is a pending interrupt, and with IE in CANCTL set the interrupt line is active until INTID returns to 0 or IE is cleared. 0x8000 means CANSTS was updated, an error or status interrupt. SIE lets changes of RXOK, TXOK and LEC interrupt; EIE lets changes of BOFF and EWARN interrupt; IE gates everything to the interrupt controller, though CANINT updates regardless. CANMSGnINT shows every object with a pending interrupt. Setting CLRINTPND in CANIFnCMSK reads a message and clears its INTPND in one step, after which CANINT names the next pending object.

TEST in CANCTL enables CANTST, whose TX[1:0], LBACK, SILENT and BASIC bits select diagnostics and whose RX bit shows CANnRX; with TEST clear all CANTST functions are off. Silent: receives valid data and remote frames but sends only recessive bits and cannot start a transmission; dominant bits it should send (ACK, overload, active error flags) are looped back inside, so bus traffic can be watched untouched. Loopback: CANnTX is routed to CANnRX inside, own messages are received and stored if they pass the filter, acknowledge errors are ignored, the real CANnRX is ignored, and CANnTX shows the messages. Loopback with silent: CANnRX is disconnected and CANnTX held recessive, for testing without disturbing a live bus.

BASIC in CANTST runs the controller without the message RAM. The CANIF1 registers are the transmit buffer: setting BUSY in CANIF1CRQ requests a transmission and locks them; when the bus is idle they load into the shift register and send, and BUSY clears on completion. Clearing BUSY while locked aborts and disables retransmission after lost arbitration or error. The CANIF2 registers are the receive buffer: each received message is stored without filtering, and setting BUSY in CANIF2CRQ copies the shift register into them, so the transfer can be watched. Message-object control and status bits, the CANIFnCMSK control bits and the message number are not used; in CANIF2MCTL NEWDAT and MSGLST keep their function, DLC[3:0] shows the received DLC and the other control bits are clear.

TX[1:0] in CANTST sets CANnTX: controlled by the CAN controller, driving the sample point to show bit timing, driven low, or driven high. The last two, with CANnRX readable, test the physical layer. The three test settings disturb all protocol functions; TX[1:0] must be 0 for message transfer, loopback, silent or basic mode.

Small bit-timing errors may not fail at once but can badly reduce network performance; bit synchronization often covers a wrong setting so that only occasional error frames appear, but during arbitration a misplaced sample point can drive a transmitter error passive. Rates run from below 1 kbps to 1000 kbps. Each node has its own clock and sets its bit-time parameters so all share one bit rate; nodes resynchronize to the bit stream to absorb oscillator drift within tolerance. The bit time has four segments of programmable numbers of time quanta: Sync, where bus edges are expected (an edge outside it has a phase error); Prop, for physical delays in the network; and Phase1 and Phase2 around the sample point. SJW limits how far resynchronization moves the sample point within the phase segments. TSEG1 = Prop + Phase1 and TSEG2 = Phase2; Phase1 = Phase2 or Phase1 + 1 = Phase2. A rate can be met by several settings; delays and oscillator tolerance decide which works.

BRP sets the time quantum and TSEG1, TSEG2 and SJW the number of quanta per bit; bit timing, sample point and synchronization are evaluated once per quantum. The controller builds and takes apart frames, adds and removes fixed-format and stuff bits, computes and checks the CRC, handles errors and picks the synchronization type. Each bit is sampled or driven at the sample point. The time after it needed to work out the next bit, the information processing time (IPT), may be at most 2 tq; this controller's IPT is 0 tq. It is the lower limit for Phase2; synchronization may shorten Phase2 below it without affecting bus timing.

Start from the bit rate; the bit time (1/bit rate) must be a whole number of system clock periods and 4 to 25 quanta long. Prop comes first, from measured delays (for an expandable bus, a maximum bus length and node delay), rounded up to whole quanta. Sync is 1 tq, leaving bit time - Prop - 1 quanta for the phase segments: equal if even, else Phase2 = Phase1 + 1. Phase2 may not be shorter than the IPT (0 to 2 tq by implementation). SJW is the least of 4, Phase1 and Phase2. Where several settings work, choose the one with the widest oscillator tolerance. Nodes with different clocks need different settings for one rate; propagation time is worked out once for the whole network from the slowest nodes, and the network's tolerance is that of its least tolerant node. The result may call for a shorter bus, a lower rate or more stable oscillators.

Two independent comparators, each comparing two analog voltages and giving a logic result. A comparator can drive a device pin in place of a board comparator (not every comparator has an output pin), interrupt the application, or start an ADC sample sequence; interrupt and ADC trigger logic are separate, so one can act on a rising edge and the other on a falling edge. Each compares an external pin with another external pin or with the internal programmable reference; the test voltage can be compared with its own external reference, a shared external reference, or the shared internal reference.

Each comparator has a negative input Cn-, a positive input Cn+, an alternate positive input and the reference input, with ACCTLn and ACSTATn, and gives an output, a trigger and an interrupt; the voltage reference is set by ACREFCTL and interrupts by ACRIS, ACMIS and ACINTEN.

VOUT = 1 when VIN- < VIN+ and 0 when VIN- > VIN+. VIN- is the external input Cn-; VIN+ is Cn+, C0+ or the internal reference VIREF, selected in ACCTL, and CINV can invert the output before the interrupt and trigger generators. ACCTL and ACSTAT set up each comparator, ACREFCTL the internal reference, and ACMIS, ACRIS and ACINTEN the interrupts. The output usually raises an interrupt under ISEN in ACCTL; it can also drive the Cno pin or trigger the ADC. The ASRCP bits in ACCTL must be set before the comparators are used.

A resistor ladder with a decoder, set by ACREFCTL. RNG clear selects the high range, RNG set the low range; each range has 16 thresholds chosen by the VREF field. High range: from VDDA/4.2 in steps of VDDA/29.4. Low range: from 0 V in steps of VDDA/22.12. With EN clear the reference is 0 V (GND) for any VREF; RNG = 1 and VREF = 0 then keep noise on the reference ground lowest. The values are ideal; each step varies between a minimum and maximum with process and temperature. The VDDA = 3.3 V tables scale with VDDA.

To read a comparator's output from its register: write 0x0000.0001 to RCGCACMP; enable the GPIO ports' clocks in RCGCGPIO; set the input pins as GPIO inputs; set the PMCn fields of GPIOPCTL for the outputs; write 0x0000.030C to ACREFCTL for a 1.65 V internal reference; write 0x0000.040C to ACCTLn to use the internal reference without inversion; wait 10 µs; read OVAL in ACSTATn, which follows the level on C-. The comparators are at 0x4003.C000; after their clock is enabled, 3 system clocks must pass before their registers are accessed.

Out of reset most pins are tri-stated GPIOs. GPIOAMSEL selects analog mode; a digital alternate function needs its pin's GPIOAFSEL bit set and the PMCx field of GPIOPCTL set to the function's encoding. The pins of the special-considerations table come out of reset in their listed function and return to it on power-on reset or RST.

Stress beyond the absolute maximum ratings can damage the part permanently, and long exposure at those limits can reduce its reliability. Operation at the ratings themselves is not guaranteed.
